negation-ne-pas.intro_tr: In French, the basic way to make a sentence negative is to place the particles "ne" and "pas" on both sides of the verb: subject + ne + verb + pas. This structure is not formed with a single word like "don't/doesn't" in English, but with two particles that surround the verb like a "sandwich," which is why it may seem unfamiliar at first for Turkish speakers. "ne" shortens to "n'" before verbs beginning with a vowel or silent h. In compound tenses like Passé composé, "ne...pas" surrounds the auxiliary verb (avoir/être), leaving the past participle outside. In everyday spoken language, "ne" is often dropped and only "pas" is used (Je sais pas.), but in written language and exams, both must always be written together.

subject-pronouns.intro_tr: In French, it is mandatory to use a subject pronoun in every sentence; unlike in Turkish, it is not sufficient to understand the subject from verb conjugation, because many verb forms sound the same to the ear. There are nine basic subject pronouns: je, tu, il, elle, on, nous, vous, ils, elles. Of these, "il/elle" and "ils/elles" are used for both people and objects (depending on the gender of the noun) — this is an important point that distinguishes French from Turkish. "On" is a very versatile pronoun frequently used instead of "nous" in everyday conversation. On this page you will find the complete list of pronouns, the tu/vous distinction, the areas of use of "on", and common mistakes in table form.

etre-avoir.intro_tr: être (to be) and avoir (to have) are the two most frequently used and most irregularly conjugated verbs in French; therefore, memorizing their conjugations is the first and most important step at the A1 level. être is used when expressing "what/how something is" such as identity, condition, profession, nationality; avoir, on the other hand, indicates possession but in French many conditions (including those expressed with "-im" in Turkish) are also constructed with avoir, such as age, hunger, coldness. Additionally, both verbs, in the passé composé (past tense) conjugation, accompany other verbs as auxiliary verbs (auxiliaire) — therefore, past tense cannot be constructed without knowing their conjugations. On this page, the present tense, negative and question forms of both verbs, common avoir expressions, and the most frequently confused points are presented in table form.

prepositions-basic.title_tr: Basic Prepositions (à, de, en, chez) and Contractions (au, du)
prepositions-basic.intro_tr: In French, à, de, en, and chez are four of the most frequently used basic prepositions; they establish relationships of place, direction, origin, possession, and time. When the prepositions à and de encounter the definite articles le and les, they do not remain separate but "merge" into single words like au, du, aux (contraction); this contraction is mandatory in French, forms like "à le" or "de les" are incorrect. Before la and l', there is never a contraction. en and chez, however, never merge with articles and generally have their own unique rules (especially with country names and indicating person/profession). On this page you will find the functions of the four prepositions, a contraction table, their usage with country/city names, and common mistakes.

tables.caption_tr: Contraction of à and de with Articles (au, du, aux, des)
footnotes_tr: Rule: à/de + le → au/du; à/de + les → aux/des. There is never a contraction before la or l'.
The forms "à le", "à les", "de le", "de les" are INCORRECT in French, au/aux/du/des must be used.

gender-of-nouns.intro_tr: In French, every noun is necessarily either masculine (masculin) or feminine (féminin), and this gender is mostly not logical but rather historical/structural in nature; therefore every word must be memorized together with its gender. The gender of the noun is determined by the article preceding it (le/la), the agreement of adjectives, and certain pronouns. Some suffixes at the end of words (-age, -ment masculine; -tion, -té, -ée feminine, for example) provide strong clues but there are numerous exceptions. Some nouns gain a completely different meaning when used in masculine or feminine form (le livre = book, la livre = pound/kilo, for example). In certain semantic categories such as countries, days, languages, professions, there are also quite regular patterns.

adjective-agreement.intro_tr: In French, adjectives agree with the nouns they modify in gender (masculine/feminine) and number (singular/plural); that is, the adjective changes like the noun. Unlike Turkish, the vast majority of adjectives in French come AFTER the noun (une voiture rouge), but a small group of common and short adjectives (BAGS: Beauty, Age, Goodness, Size) come BEFORE the noun (un petit chat). Some adjectives take on a completely different meaning depending on whether they come before or after the noun (ancien, grand, pauvre, etc.). There are many regular and irregular patterns in forming feminine and plural forms; memorizing them is the foundation of fluent speech.

er-verbs-present.title_tr: Present Tense of -er Verbs (Présent des verbes en -er)
er-verbs-present.intro_tr: Approximately 90% of French verbs end in -er and this group is called "1st group verbs (1er groupe)"; all conjugate according to the same regular pattern (only exception: aller). To form the present tense (présent), the -er ending in the infinitive is removed, the remaining part becomes the "root (radical)" and to this root, the endings -e, -es, -e, -ons, -ez, -ent are added according to the subject. The singular persons (je, tu, il/elle/on) and the ils/elles plural sound EXACTLY the same to the ear because the -e, -es, -ent endings are not pronounced — this is one of the most confusing points when learning French. Some -er verbs (commencer, manger, acheter, préférer, appeler, payer and so on) show minor but regular changes in spelling; these are also covered in a separate table. This page summarizes regular conjugation, spelling/pronunciation exceptions, and frequently used verbs at a glance.

aller-venir.title_tr: aller and venir; Near Future (aller + infinitive)
aller-venir.intro_tr: "aller" (to go) and "venir" (to come) are the two most frequently used irregular verbs in French and are used both to express movement on their own and to construct tense structures. The pattern "aller" + infinitive (infinitif) forms the "futur proche" (near future) structure, which corresponds to the future tense "-ecek/-acak" in Turkish; for example, "je vais manger" = "I will eat". In contrast, the pattern "venir de" + infinitive constructs the "passé récent" (near past) structure, which means "I just did". Both verbs are irregular conjugations, so you need to memorize all personal forms. Furthermore, when "aller" is used with city/country names, it takes different prepositions (à, en, au, aux, chez).

tables.caption_tr: The present tense (présent) conjugation of the "aller" (to go) verb
footnotes_tr: Although "aller" ends with -er, it is conjugated completely irregularly; its root changes in each person (v-, all-).

tables.caption_tr: The present tense (présent) conjugation of the "venir" (to come) verb
footnotes_tr: Verbs like "revenir" (to come back), "devenir" (to become), "tenir" (to hold) follow the same irregular pattern.

tables.caption_tr: Near future (futur proche): aller (present tense) + infinitive
footnotes_tr: No preposition (à, de) is used before the infinitive: "je vais à manger" WRONG, "je vais manger" CORRECT.
Negative structure: subject + ne + aller + pas + infinitive → "Je ne vais pas partir." (I will not go.)

tables.caption_tr: Near past (passé récent): venir de + infinitive
footnotes_tr: "de" becomes "d'" before infinitives starting with a vowel (d'arriver, d'appeler).
Although this structure is past tense, the verb (venir) is always conjugated in the PRESENT tense.

aller au travail / à la piscine

possessive-adjectives.intro_tr: Possessive adjectives (mon, ma, mes, etc.) in French indicate the owner of a noun by adding the meaning of "my, your, his/her..." Unlike Turkish, in French the possessive adjective changes not according to the gender of the owner, but according to the gender and number of the POSSESSED noun — this is the point that Turkish students most often confuse. For example, "son livre" can mean both "his book" and "her book", because "livre" is a masculine noun. The possessive adjective always comes before the noun and forms a single block with it; it should not be thought of as a separate pronoun like in English/Turkish. Also, before feminine nouns starting with a vowel or silent 'h', "ma, ta, sa" change to (for ease of pronunciation) "mon, ton, son" — this rule is frequently asked in exams.

tables.caption_tr: Basic Possessive Adjectives Table (According to Owner)
Important Exception: Feminine Nouns Beginning with a Vowel / Silent 'h'
footnotes_tr: This change is only for ease of PRONUNCIATION; the noun remains feminine (it continues as feminine in agreement adjectives). Example: 'mon amie' but 'une amie chère'.
'notre', 'votre', 'leur' are not affected by this rule because they don't end in a vowel and have no separate masculine/feminine form.

footnotes_tr: In French, it is not the gender of the owner, but the gender of the POSSESSED OBJECT that is decisive. From context, it is understood which person is meant.

definite-indefinite-articles.title_tr: Articles: le / la / les, un / une / des
definite-indefinite-articles.intro_tr: In French, an article almost always appears before every noun; a noun cannot be used alone. Definite articles (le, la, les, l') are used before nouns that are known, previously mentioned, or express a general concept; indefinite articles (un, une, des), on the other hand, are used before countable nouns that are mentioned for the first time or nouns of indefinite quantity. The form the article takes depends on the gender (masculine/feminine) and number (singular/plural) of the noun. Additionally, when the prepositions à and de combine with le/les, special "contraction" (contraction) forms appear (au, aux, du, des). In negative sentences, un/une/des usually becomes "de"; this is one of the rules most commonly confused by Turkish students.

tables.caption_tr: Definite Articles (le / la / les / l')

tables.caption_tr: Indefinite Articles (un / une / des)

pronunciation-spelling.title_tr: Pronunciation and Writing (Accents, Silent Letters, Liaison)
pronunciation-spelling.intro_tr: Correct pronunciation in French requires understanding three fundamental mechanisms arising from the fact that written letters are often not pronounced as they appear: accent marks (which change the sound of letters or distinguish words), silent letters (especially consonants at the end of words are generally not pronounced), and liaison (the connection when the silent final consonant of a word is articulated as it links to the next word beginning with a vowel). In addition to these, elision (the apostrophe preventing vowel collision) and nasal vowels are also integral parts of French pronunciation. Although these rules may seem complex at first, they follow certain patterns and become automatic with regular practice. This page presents all the fundamental pronunciation and writing rules for learners starting from zero in a single reference format.

tables.caption_tr: Accent Marks (Les Accents)
rows: Kapalı 'e' sesi /e/ verir, sadece e üzerinde kullanılır
Ses değiştirmez, sadece aynı yazılan kelimeleri ayırt eder
Açık/uzun 'e' sesi verir; genelde tarihsel bir 's' harfinin yerini tutar
Genelde eski bir 's' harfinin izidir, sesi hafif uzatır
İki bitişik ünlünün AYRI ayrı okunduğunu gösterir
c harfinin a/o/u önünde /s/ okunmasını sağlar (normalde /k/ olurdu)
footnotes_tr: Accents in French are not optional decorations; they are a mandatory part of correct spelling; their omission is considered a spelling error.

Fransızcada h HİÇBİR ZAMAN kendi başına okunmaz

Mastar fiillerde -er sonu /e/ olarak okunur (r okunmaz)

ir-re-verbs-present.intro_tr: In French, verbs are divided into three major groups according to their infinitive endings: -er, -ir, and -re. This page covers the present tense (présent) conjugation of -ir and -re verbs. -ir verbs are further subdivided into three types: finir type (the most numerous group that takes the '-iss-' suffix in plural), partir type (a short-stem group that drops the stem consonant in singular persons), and ouvrir type (an exceptional group actually conjugated like -er verbs). -re verbs generally follow the regular vendre type pattern; however, some frequently used -re verbs like prendre, mettre, dire are irregular verbs showing stem changes. The tables below present all subgroups, full conjugations, suffix summaries, and common mistakes together.

tables.caption_tr: 1. -IR Verbs: finir Type (-iss- Regular Group) — Full Conjugation
footnotes_tr: This group is the largest -ir verb group; in plural persons the stem takes the '-iss-' suffix (nous finISSons).
Other examples: remplir (to fill), bâtir (to build), obéir (to obey), réfléchir (to think/reflect), rougir (to blush).

tables.caption_tr: 2. -IR Verbs: partir Type (Short-stem Group) — Full Conjugation
footnotes_tr: In singular persons (je, tu, il) the stem-final consonant drops: dor(m)s, par(t)s, ser(v)s.
In plural the stem consonant returns and regular suffixes are added.
Other examples: sentir (to feel/smell), mentir (to lie).

tables.caption_tr: 3. -RE Verbs: vendre Type (Regular Group) — Full Conjugation
footnotes_tr: In 3rd singular person (il/elle/on) no extra suffix is added; the stem already ends in 'd' (vend, attend, répond).
Other examples: descendre (to go down), rendre (to give back), entendre (to hear), tondre (to mow).

tables.caption_tr: 4. Important Exception: ouvrir Group (-ir Verb But Conjugated Like -er!)
footnotes_tr: Although these verbs end in the -ir infinitive, their suffixes are exactly like -er verbs (-e, -es, -e, -ons, -ez, -ent).
Another example: cueillir (to pick/gather) is similarly conjugated: je cueille, nous cueillons.

tables.caption_tr: 5. Frequently Used Irregular -ir / -re Verbs — Full Conjugation
footnotes_tr: vous dites (NOT vous disez) and in prendre a double 'n' in ils/elles (prennent) are exceptions requiring attention.
In the verb boire the stem changes in nous/vous/ils: bois- → buv-/boiv-.

plural-forms.intro_tr: In French, the plural of nouns is generally formed by adding -s to the singular form, but this -s is often not pronounced (it appears in written form, but in spoken language the article usually indicates the plural: le → les, un → des). Some groups of nouns follow different rules: those already ending in -s/-x/-z do not change, those ending in -au/-eu/-eau take -x, those ending in -al usually become -aux. Additionally, there are completely irregular plurals and special rules for compound nouns. This page collects all these rules and exceptions in one place.

tables.caption_tr: 1. General Rule: Singular Noun + -s
rows: Çoğulu ayırt eden şey tanımlıktır (une → des)
Sesli harfle biten isimlerde de kural aynıdır
footnotes_tr: The final -s is almost never pronounced. When speaking, what helps us understand the plural is not the noun itself, but the article or adjective before it (le/la → les, un/une → des, ce/cette → ces).

tables.caption_tr: 2. Already Ending in -s, -x, -z: No Change
footnotes_tr: Rule: To nouns already ending in -s, -x, or -z, nothing is added; the singular and plural spelling are the same.

tables.caption_tr: 3. Ending in -au, -eau, -eu: +x
footnotes_tr: pneu and bleu are exceptions to this rule and normally take only -s (les pneus, les bleus).

tables.caption_tr: 4. Ending in -al: -aux
footnotes_tr: Rule: -al → -aux. However, some -al nouns shown in the table below are exceptions and take only -s.

tables.caption_tr: 5. Exceptions to the -al Rule: Those Taking Only -s
footnotes_tr: These words must be memorized; they do not follow the -aux rule.

tables.caption_tr: 6. Ending in -ail: Generally +s, Some -aux
footnotes_tr: The majority of those ending in -ail are regular (+s), but a few commonly used words like travail, vitrail, corail, bail take -aux.

tables.caption_tr: 7. Completely Irregular Plurals
footnotes_tr: Although the plural of ciel is usually 'cieux' (in literary/figurative sense), 'ciels' can sometimes be used in the sense of concrete sky (e.g., 'les ciels de Paris').

tables.caption_tr: 8. Plural in Compound Nouns (Noms Composés)
rows: Her iki öğe de çoğul olur
Her iki öğe de çoğul olur
Sadece ilk isim çoğul olur, ikinci isim değişmez
Fiil değişmez, isim genelde çoğul olur (anlam çoklu ise)
footnotes_tr: In compound nouns, plural rules vary depending on the type of word (noun, adjective, verb, preposition); since there is no fixed rule, it is safest to memorize the commonly used ones.

tables.caption_tr: 9. Nouns Used Only in Plural or Those Taking Special Meaning
footnotes_tr: Some French nouns are used only in plural form and their singular forms either do not exist or carry a completely different meaning.

question-formation.title_tr: Question Sentences: Est-ce que, Intonation, Inverted Structure
question-formation.intro_tr: In French, there are three main ways to ask a yes/no question: raising the pitch of your voice (intonation), adding "est-ce que" to the beginning of the sentence, or changing the position of the subject and verb (inverted structure/inversion). These three methods carry the same meaning but the contexts in which they are used (everyday conversation / neutral / formal-written language) are different. In questions using a question word (qui, que, où, quand, comment, pourquoi, combien, quel), the same three structures also apply; only the question word is added to the beginning of the sentence. In inverted structure, when the subject il/elle/on combines with a verb ending in a vowel sound, a "-t-" is inserted in between; this is to make pronunciation easier. For a beginner student, the easiest and most common method is "est-ce que", while in everyday conversation intonation is preferred, and in written/formal language inverted structure is preferred.

partitive-articles.intro_tr: Partitive article (article partitif), is used in French when speaking of an indefinite/uncountable part of a whole: 'some bread', 'some water' for example. It is formed from the combination of the preposition 'de' with the articles le/la/les and takes the forms du, de la, de l', des. It is generally used with food, drink and abstract concepts (du courage, de la patience for example). In negative sentences these articles almost always become 'de/d''. For countable singular objects, on the other hand, 'un/une' (indefinite article) is used — this is a point frequently confused with the partitive article.

tables.caption_tr: Forms of the Partitive Article
footnotes_tr: The plural 'des' can be both the plural of the indefinite article (un/une → des) and the plural of the partitive article; it is understood from context.
For nouns beginning with silent h and vowels, 'de l'' is always used regardless of gender.

tables.caption_tr: Comparison of Article Types
footnotes_tr: The same noun (café, pain, eau...) can be used with any of the three article types depending on context.

footnotes_tr: Rule: in negative sentences du/de la/de l'/des → becomes only 'de' (d' before a vowel).
EXCEPTION: in sentences constructed with the verb être, the partitive article does not change → 'Ce n'est pas du café' (not 'Ce n'est pas de café').
If quantity is specified (beaucoup de, pas de... but with a number), then 'de' is still used: in cases like 'Je n'ai pas trois pommes' the rule does not apply, this is a different structure.

numbers-time.intro_tr: In French, numbers and telling time are quite different from Turkish and follow irregular rules — particularly numbers like 70, 80, 90 are constructed using the logic "60+10", "4×20", "4×20+10" and require memorization. When telling time, in daily conversation a 12-hour system is used (et quart, et demie, moins le quart), while in formal settings (train, airplane, TV) a 24-hour system is used. The word "Heure" is feminine, which is why "une heure" is used; "demi" remains masculine with midi/minuit but becomes feminine with heure (demie). This page compiles numbers from 0-100, large numbers, ordinal numbers, time-telling patterns, and the most common mistakes all in one place.

passe-compose-avoir.intro_tr: Passé composé is the most common past tense in French used to describe events completed in the past, occurring at a specific moment, or consecutive events. The vast majority of verbs form this tense with the auxiliary verb "avoir" + participe passé (past participle); only certain verbs indicating movement/state and reflexive verbs take "être" (this topic is covered in a separate section). When formed with "avoir," the participle normally does NOT agree with the subject, but only with the direct object (COD) if it precedes the verb. This page summarizes the auxiliary verb conjugation, regular/irregular participle formation, negative-interrogative patterns, and the agreement rule in table form.

imperative-mood.intro_tr: Imperative mood (l'impératif) is used to give someone a direct command, request, suggestion or instruction. In French, the imperative mood has only 3 conjugations: tu, nous and vous — the subject pronoun (such as je, il, elle, ils) is never spoken or written, only the verb conjugation is used. The imperative mood is generally derived from the present tense (présent) conjugation, but in -er verbs the -s ending at the end of the tu form is dropped. In reflexive verbs and sentences using object pronouns, the position of the pronoun changes depending on whether the sentence is affirmative or negative; this is the point that confuses students the most. The imperative mood of être, avoir, savoir and vouloir verbs is irregular and must be memorized.

passe-compose-vs-imparfait.intro_tr: In French, the two most commonly used tenses for narrating events in the past are passé composé and imparfait; even though both tell the "past," their functions are completely different. Passé composé describes actions with clear beginning and end, single occurrences or consecutive completed actions — it answers the question "what happened?". Imparfait, on the other hand, describes situations that were ongoing in the past, habits, descriptions (weather, time, age, emotion, setting) — it answers the question "how was it, what was being done?". In most cases, both are used together in one sentence: imparfait paints the background (setting), while passé composé reports the event that suddenly intervenes in that background. Moreover, some verbs like savoir, connaître, vouloir, pouvoir, devoir change in meaning even when used in these two tenses; therefore, these verbs must be memorized separately.

adverb-formation.intro_tr: In French, the vast majority of adverbs are derived from adjectives by adding the -ment suffix; this is a structure similar in meaning to the "-ce/-ca" or "in a way" construction in Turkish. How the suffix is added depends on the letter the adjective ends with: sometimes -ment is added to the feminine form, sometimes to the masculine form, and sometimes special -amment/-emment patterns are used. Also, some frequently used adjectives like bon, mauvais, petit have completely irregular adverb forms (bien, mal, peu). The placement of the adverb in the sentence is also important: in simple tenses it comes immediately after the verb, in compound tenses it comes either between the auxiliary verb and the past participle or after the past participle depending on the length of the adverb. This page summarizes both the derivation rules and the placement rules in table form.

modal-verbs.title_tr: pouvoir, devoir, vouloir, savoir — Basic Modal Verbs
modal-verbs.intro_tr: pouvoir, devoir, vouloir and savoir are the four basic "modal" verbs of French; used together with the infinitive form of another verb, they express concepts such as possibility, obligation, wish, and knowledge/ability (like Je peux partir, Il doit venir). All are irregularly conjugated and follow a similar pattern in singular persons (je, tu, il): root + -x/-x/-t or -s/-s/-t. devoir is particularly important because it can carry both "obligation" and, depending on the tense, "assumption," "recommendation," and "regret" meanings. pouvoir and savoir are often confused: pouvoir means immediate possibility/permission, while savoir means learned skill or knowledge. The conditional mood of vouloir (je voudrais) is almost mandatory in everyday speech to politely express a wish.

tables.caption_tr: 1. Present Tense (Présent) — Complete Conjugation
footnotes_tr: In singular persons (je/tu/il), the root changes and takes the ending -x, -x, -t (except devoir: je dois, tu dois, il doit → -s, -s, -t).
In nous/vous forms, the root is different and regular endings are used: -ons, -ez.
In the ils/elles form, the root is the same as the present tense's 'strong root' and takes the -ent ending (peuvent, doivent, veulent, savent).

tables.caption_tr: 2. Conjugation Roots in Other Basic Tenses (with je)
footnotes_tr: All four verbs are conjugated with the auxiliary verb avoir in the passé composé.
The roots of futur and conditionnel are irregular: pourr-, devr-, voudr-, saur- (should not be confused with the infinitive root).

demonstratives.title_tr: Demonstrative Adjectives and Pronouns (ce, cette, celui)
demonstratives.intro_tr: Demonstrative adjectives (ce, cet, cette, ces) come immediately before a noun, adding the meaning "this/that" and must agree with the noun they modify in terms of gender and number; demonstrative pronouns (celui, celle, ceux, celles), on the other hand, replace a noun mentioned earlier and cannot be used alone—they must always be supported with the suffix -ci/-là, with a preposition (de), or with a relative clause (qui, que, dont). In French, the distinction between "this" and "that" in Turkish does not exist structurally; the difference in proximity-distance is indicated only by the suffixes -ci (near) and -là (far), otherwise both mean only "this/that". Additionally, neutral (gender-neutral) demonstrative pronouns such as ceci, cela, ça, ce do not refer to a specific noun but to an idea, sentence, or situation, and are especially frequently used with the c'est pattern. For a student starting from zero level, the most critical point is to use cet instead of ce before masculine singular nouns beginning with a vowel or silent h, and never to leave pronouns alone.

tables.caption_tr: Demonstrative Adjectives (Adjectifs démonstratifs) — ce, cet, cette, ces
rows: Ünsüz harfle başlayan eril isimlerden önce
Eril tekil (sesli harf/sessiz h ile başlayan isim)
a, e, i, o, u veya sessiz h ile başlayan eril isimlerden önce (liaison zorunlu)
Her dişil isimden önce (sesli harfle başlasa bile)
Tüm çoğul isimlerden önce, cinsiyet ayrımı yoktur
footnotes_tr: If proximity/distance is to be emphasized, the suffix -ci or -là is added to the noun: ce livre-ci (this book), ce livre-là (that book).
cet is masculine singular only; in the feminine, cette is always used, and it does not change before a vowel (cette histoire).

tables.caption_tr: Demonstrative Pronouns (Pronoms démonstratifs) — Simple and Compound Forms
rows: celui-ci est neuf, celui-là est vieux
celle-ci me plaît plus que celle-là
footnotes_tr: Simple forms (celui, celle, ceux, celles) cannot be used alone; they must always be completed with -ci/-là, de + noun, or with qui/que/dont.
-ci = 'this' (near/recently mentioned), -là = 'that' (far/previously mentioned); it is frequently used when comparing two objects.

tables.caption_tr: Neutral Demonstrative Pronouns — ce, ceci, cela, ça
rows: être fiili ile birlikte (c'est, ce sont, c'était)
C'est important. / Ce sont mes amis.
Belirli bir isme değil genel duruma gönderme yapar
Yazı dilinde, yaklaşmakta olan veya yakın bir şeye işaret eder
Konuşma dilinde nadirdir, resmî/yazılı üsluba özgüdür
Soyut fikir, önceki cümle veya uzak bir duruma gönderme
Yazı dilinde ve resmî konuşmada tercih edilir
Günlük konuşma dilinde cela'nın kısaltılmış hâli
Samimi/gündelik dilde çok yaygındır, yazı dilinde kaçınılır
footnotes_tr: ceci/cela does not replace a noun; it refers to an idea, sentence, or indefinite situation.

tables.caption_tr: celui / celle / ceux / celles — Completion with de, qui, que, dont
footnotes_tr: These structures are used especially for comparison and avoiding repetition (not repeating the same noun a second time).

tables.caption_tr: Frequently Confused Structure: ce/c'est vs il/elle est
rows: Meslek, kimlik, genel değerlendirme; isim önünde makale ile
Belirli bir kişi/şey hakkında doğrudan nitelik, makalesiz sıfat

Konuşma dilinde bazen makale düşer ama yazıda önerilmez
Çoğulda être her zaman 'sont' olur, 'il/elle est' değil
footnotes_tr: Rule summary: before a noun → c'est/ce sont; before an adjective (if the person/object is already known) → il est/elle est.

futur-simple.intro_tr: Futur simple is a simple (one-word) tense used in French to express actions that will happen in the future; it corresponds to the Turkish suffix "-acak/-ecek". All verbs use the same six person endings (-ai, -as, -a, -ons, -ez, -ont), and these endings are added directly to the verb's infinitive root (sometimes a modified stem). In regular -er and -ir verbs, the stem is generally the infinitive itself, while in -re verbs the final "e" is dropped. Some frequently used verbs (être, avoir, aller, faire, venir, voir, savoir, pouvoir, vouloir, devoir...) take completely irregular stems and must be memorized. Futur simple is used for definite plans, predictions, promises, polite orders, and in patterns like "si + present tense" and "quand/dès que + futur simple".

tables.caption_tr: 1. Futur Simple Person Endings (common for all verbs)
footnotes_tr: These six endings are WITHOUT EXCEPTION the same in all verbs (regular or irregular); the only part that changes is the stem.
The endings resemble the conjugation of the verb avoir in présent tense (ai, as, a, ons, ez, ont) — this similarity makes memorization easier.

tables.caption_tr: 2. Complete Conjugation of Regular Verbs: -er, -ir, -re
footnotes_tr: In -er and -ir verbs, stem = the entire infinitive (parler-, finir-).
In -re verbs, the final 'e' is dropped: vendre -> vendr- + endings.

tables.caption_tr: 3. Most Frequently Used Irregular Stems
footnotes_tr: These stems must be memorized without fail; they cannot be derived from any rule.
Person endings (-ai, -as, -a, -ons, -ez, -ont) are added to these stems in the same way: je serai, tu iras, il pourra...

tables.caption_tr: 4. -er Verbs Showing Spelling Changes
rows: her iki biçim de kabul edilir
footnotes_tr: These changes follow the same logic as the changes seen in 'je/tu/il/ils' conjugations in présent tense.

tables.caption_tr: 5. Uses of Futur Simple
rows: Il fera plus chaud dans dix ans.
Koşullu gelecek (si'den sonra ASLA futur kullanılmaz)
Si tu viens, je serai content.
İki eylem de gelecekte gerçekleşir (Türkçedeki şimdiki zamana aldanmayın)
footnotes_tr: The most common mistake Turkish speakers make: in the sentence 'quand tu arriveras', forgetting to use futur simple for the second verb by mistaking it for present tense — in French, both verbs must be in the future.

tables.caption_tr: 6. Comparison of Futur Proche and Futur Simple
rows: Yakın, kesin, konuşma anına yakın gelecek
Yazılı ve resmî dilde tercih edilir
footnotes_tr: In spoken language, futur proche is used much more frequently; futur simple, on the other hand, is prominent in news bulletins, formal writing, and literary texts.

reflexive-verbs.title_tr: Reflexive Verbs (Les Verbes Pronominaux) — se lever, s'appeler
reflexive-verbs.intro_tr: In French, reflexive verbs (les verbes pronominaux) are verbs that show the subject performing an action on themselves and are used with the pronoun "se" (oneself) in infinitive form; for example se lever (to get up), s'appeler (to be named), se laver (to wash). When conjugating these verbs, a second pronoun that agrees with the subject (me, te, se, nous, vous, se) is added before the verb. In the past tense (passé composé) they are always conjugated with the auxiliary verb être, and in most cases gender-number agreement is made with the subject. In negative sentences, "ne" comes before the reflexive pronoun and "pas" comes after the verb. Some verbs are truly reflexive (action performed on oneself), some are reciprocal (action performed to each other), and some verbs only exist in pronominal form (such as se souvenir).

tables.caption_tr: Reflexive Pronouns (Subject + Pronoun Matching)
footnotes_tr: Before verbs beginning with a vowel or silent h, me, te, se → m', t', s': je m'appelle, tu t'habilles.
The pronoun comes IMMEDIATELY BEFORE the conjugated verb (it comes between the subject and the verb).

tables.caption_tr: se lever (To get up) — Present Tense Complete Conjugation
footnotes_tr: The verb lever shows stem change: in singular persons and 3rd plural e → è (grave accent), in nous/vous it remains unchanged — just like in -e_er verbs such as acheter, promener.

tables.caption_tr: s'appeler (To be named) — Present Tense Complete Conjugation
footnotes_tr: The verb appeler shows consonant doubling: in singular persons and 3rd plural l → ll, in nous/vous a single l remains — the same pattern as the jeter (m'appelle/jette) group.

tables.caption_tr: Negative Structure (ne ... pas with Reflexive Verbs)
rows: Je ne me lève pas tôt.
jö nö mö lev pa to
Il ne se lave pas le matin.
il nö sö lav pa lö matẽ
Nous ne nous couchons pas tard.
nu nö nu kuşõ pa tar
footnotes_tr: 'ne' comes BEFORE the reflexive pronoun; 'pas' comes AFTER the conjugated verb: ne + [me/te/se/nous/vous] + verb + pas.
In spoken language 'ne' is often dropped: Je me lève pas tôt.

tables.caption_tr: Passé Composé (Conjugation with être and Past Participle Agreement)
footnotes_tr: General rule: if the reflexive pronoun is a direct object (COD), the past participle agrees with the subject (this is the case in most verbs).

EXCEPTION: if the reflexive pronoun is an indirect object (COI) THEN AGREEMENT IS NOT MADE — for example 'elles se sont téléphoné' (se téléphoner à qqn), 'elle s'est lavé les mains' (les mains = COD, se = COI so the past participle does not change).

tables.caption_tr: Imperative Mood (Impératif) — Affirmative and Negative
footnotes_tr: In the affirmative imperative, the pronoun comes AFTER the verb and is connected with a hyphen; 'te' → 'toi'.
In the negative imperative, the pronoun remains BEFORE the verb, as in a normal sentence: ne + pronoun + verb + pas.

tables.caption_tr: Types of Reflexive Verbs (Classification by Meaning)
rows: se laver, se lever, se coiffer
İki veya daha fazla özne eylemi birbirine yapar (çoğul özne)
'se' olmadan fiil anlamsız veya çok farklı anlama gelir

Fiilin düz hali ile dönüşlü hali farklı anlam taşır

object-pronouns.intro_tr: In French, object pronouns take the place of nouns in a sentence to avoid repeating the same noun repeatedly. There are two basic types: DIRECT object pronouns (COD: le, la, les) take the place of the complement of verbs without prepositions (like "regarder quelqu'un"); INDIRECT object pronouns (COI: lui, leur) take the place of complements used with the preposition "à" and referring only to PEOPLE (like "parler à quelqu'un"). These pronouns, unlike in Turkish, do not come after the verb, but come almost always BEFORE the verb — this is the point most confusing for Turkish speakers. In the affirmative imperative, however, the rule reverses and the pronoun comes after the verb, linked with a hyphen. Also, in passé composé, when the COD pronoun comes before the verb, the past participle (participe passé) agrees with it in gender and number; with COI (lui/leur) there is NEVER agreement.

tables.caption_tr: Direct Object Pronouns (COD) — Complete List
footnotes_tr: le and la become l' before verbs starting with a vowel or silent h: Je l'aime, not Je l'habite but for example Je l'adore.

tables.caption_tr: Indirect Object Pronouns (COI) — lui, leur and Others
footnotes_tr: lui means both 'to him' (masculine) and 'to her' (feminine) — there is NO gender distinction, this is one of the most common mistakes Turkish speakers make.
lui/leur are used ONLY for people. If referring to an OBJECT, the 'y' pronoun is used (for example: Je réponds à la lettre → J'y réponds, not lui).

tables.caption_tr: COD or COI? Decision Table Based on the Verb
footnotes_tr: Rule: If the verb takes a person/object directly (without a preposition) → COD. If the verb takes a person with 'à' → COI.

tables.caption_tr: Position of the Pronoun in the Sentence (According to Tense and Structure)
rows: Zamir fiilden SONRA, tire (-) ile bağlanır
Ne le regarde pas ! / Ne lui parle pas !
footnotes_tr: In the affirmative imperative, me → moi, te → toi: Regarde-moi ! (Look at me!)

tables.caption_tr: Agreement of the Past Participle (Participe Passé) in Passé Composé
rows: Je lui ai parlé. (değişmez, cinsiyet/sayı önemsiz)
footnotes_tr: This agreement rule applies only when the COD comes BEFORE the verb; in normal order (J'ai vu le livre) there is no agreement.
At an advanced level, this topic is detailed under the heading 'Advanced Past Participle Agreement'.

impersonal-expressions.title_tr: Impersonal Structures (il y a, il faut, weather)
impersonal-expressions.intro_tr: Impersonal structures (les tournures impersonnelles) are expressions constructed with the pronoun "il" that does not represent a specific subject but serves only a grammatical function; this "il" does not refer to any person or object. The three most frequently used structures are: "il y a" which expresses existence (there is/there are), "il faut" which expresses necessity (must/necessary), and weather-describing expressions such as "il fait / il pleut / il neige". These structures are always conjugated in the 3rd person singular (il), and even if the noun following them is plural, the verb NEVER becomes plural (for example, "il y a des livres" — "livres" is plural but "il y a" remains unchanged). In the tables below, you will find the conjugations of these three main structures in all tenses, weather patterns, and other commonly used impersonal expressions (il semble, il vaut mieux, il suffit de, etc.).

tables.caption_tr: "il y a" (there is/are) Structure's Conjugation by Tense
footnotes_tr: "il y a" is never plural: "il y a", not "il y ont" — because "avoir" here is always conjugated in the 3rd person singular.

tables.caption_tr: "il faut" (must/necessary) Structures and Uses
rows: Belirli bir kişiye yönelik zorunluluk, subjonctif zorunlu
Il ne faut pas fumer ici.
footnotes_tr: The verb "falloir" is conjugated only with the subject "il" and does not take any other subject.
"il faut que" always requires the subjunctive: "Il faut que tu sois à l'heure."

tables.caption_tr: Weather Expressions
rows: Il y a du vent. / Il vente.
il ya dü van / il vant
footnotes_tr: Weather verbs (pleuvoir, neiger) are conjugated only with "il" and do not take any other subject except in metaphorical usage.
When using "il fait" + adjective, the pattern "il y a" + noun (du soleil, du vent, du brouillard) is also common.

tables.caption_tr: Other Frequently Used Impersonal Structures
Common Mistakes and Important Points to Note
rows: Il y a des livres sont sur la table.
Il y a des livres sur la table.
"il y a" tek başına özne+yüklem görevi görür; ekstra fiil (sont) eklenmez
Il y ont beaucoup de gens.
Il y a beaucoup de gens.
"il y a" hiçbir zaman çoğul olmaz, konu ne olursa olsun "a" kalır
"il faut que" sonrası subjonctif gerekir, indicatif kullanılmaz
"il fait" sadece sıfatlarla (beau, froid, chaud) kullanılır; pleuvoir/neiger gibi fiillerle birlikte kullanılmaz
Il fait beau temps. / Il fait beau.
"il y a" varlık bildirir, hava durumu tanımlamak için "il fait" kullanılmalıdır
Belirli bir özneye yönelik zorunlulukta "que" bağlacı zorunludur

comparatives.title_tr: Comparison and Superiority (plus... que, le plus)
comparatives.intro_tr: In French, three basic structures are used to make comparisons: superiority (plus... que — more), equality (aussi... que — as), and inferiority (moins... que — less). These structures can be used with adjectives, adverbs, nouns, and verbs; the pattern changes slightly depending on each form type. The superlative degree (superlative degree / le superlatif) is formed with "le/la/les plus" or "le/la/les moins" and generally a group is indicated with "de" (e.g. "de la classe" = the most ... of the class). Some adjectives and adverbs (bon, bien, mauvais, petit) have irregular comparison and superlative forms and these must be memorized. In the tables below, all structures, irregular forms, and commonly made mistakes are summarized with examples.

tables.caption_tr: Comparison with Adjectives (superiority / equality / inferiority)
rows: Il est plus grand que moi.
Elle est aussi intelligente que lui.
Ce sac est moins lourd que l'autre.
Bu çanta diğerinden daha az ağır.
footnotes_tr: The adjective always agrees in gender and number with the compared subject: plus grande, plus grands, plus grandes.

tables.caption_tr: Comparison with Adverbs
rows: Il court plus vite que moi.
Elle parle aussi doucement que sa mère.
Il conduit moins prudemment que son frère.
O, kardeşinden daha az dikkatli araba kullanıyor.
footnotes_tr: Adverbs, unlike adjectives, do not change (do not agree).

tables.caption_tr: Comparison with Nouns (quantity)
rows: J'ai plus de temps que toi.
Elle a autant d'argent que moi.
Il y a moins d'élèves que l'an dernier.
Geçen yıla göre daha az öğrenci var.
footnotes_tr: Here 'plus/moins/autant' is used with the noun, not as an adjective, so 'de' (d') comes, not 'que' directly as in the structure used with adjectives.

tables.caption_tr: Comparison with Verbs
rows: Elle dort autant que son chat.
Biz sizden daha az seyahat ediyoruz.
footnotes_tr: In comparison made with verbs, 'de' is NOT USED as in the noun structure: 'autant que', 'plus que', 'moins que'.

tables.caption_tr: Superlative Degree — le/la/les plus / moins (Superlatif)
rows: C'est la ville la plus peuplée de France.
C'est le plus grand pays d'Europe.
C'est elle qui court le plus vite.
le plus de / le moins de + isim
C'est lui qui a le plus d'amis.
C'est ce plat qui coûte le plus.

passe-compose-etre.title_tr: être with Passé Composé and Participle Agreement
passe-compose-etre.intro_tr: In French, the passé composé is constructed with the auxiliary verb avoir for most verbs; however, a small group of verbs indicating movement, change of state, birth, or death, as well as ALL reflexive (pronominal) verbs, are conjugated with the auxiliary verb être. In the passé composé constructed with être, the past participle (participe passé), just like an adjective, agrees with the SUBJECT in gender (masculine/feminine) and number (singular/plural). These 16 essential verbs are typically memorized in French teaching with the abbreviation "Maison d'Être" or "DR & MRS VANDERTRAMP". In reflexive verbs, the agreement rule is somewhat different: if the reflexive pronoun is a direct object, agreement occurs; if it is an indirect object, no agreement occurs. Some verbs (monter, descendre, sortir, passer, retourner) can be conjugated with both être and avoir; this depends on whether the verb is used transitively or intransitively.

tables.caption_tr: 16 Essential Verbs Conjugated with être (Maison d'Être / DR & MRS VANDERTRAMP)
footnotes_tr: The prefixed derivatives of these verbs (repartir, redevenir, ressortir, etc.) are also conjugated with être.

tables.caption_tr: Complete Conjugation of aller in Passé Composé
footnotes_tr: *If on expresses a plural/mixed group, the participle can also be written in plural form as 'allés' (common in everyday speech).
If vous expresses singular politeness, the participle remains singular: Vous êtes allé, Monsieur.

tables.caption_tr: Participle Agreement (Accord du Participe Passé) - General Rule
footnotes_tr: This rule applies only to verbs conjugated with être; in verbs conjugated with avoir, the participle generally does not change.

tables.caption_tr: être + Agreement in Reflexive (Pronominal) Verbs: se lever

footnotes_tr: Other être verbs (aller→allé, entrer→entré, monter→monté, tomber→tombé, rester→resté, arriver→arrivé, rentrer→rentré, retourner→retourné, descendre→descendu) take regular participles according to the -er/-re rules.

quantifiers.title_tr: Quantity Expressions (beaucoup de, assez de, trop de)
quantifiers.intro_tr: In French, to indicate the quantity of something, quantitative adverbs such as "beaucoup de" (much), "assez de" (enough), "trop de" (too much), "un peu de" (a little), and "peu de" (little) are used. When a noun comes after these adverbs, the article (le, la, les, un, une, du, de la, des) before the noun COMPLETELY DROPS and is replaced by only "de" ("d'" before a vowel or silent "h"). This rule works the same way both with countable nouns (beaucoup de livres = many books) and with uncountable nouns (beaucoup de patience = much patience). Except for a few exceptions like "Bien des" and "la plupart des", after a quantity expression one should never use "du", "de la", or "des" — this is one of the most common mistakes made by Turkish-speaking students. Measurement and container expressions (un kilo de, une bouteille de, un verre de) also follow exactly the same "de" rule.

tables.caption_tr: Basic Quantity Adverbs + de
rows: Fazlalığın rahatsız edici olduğunu ima eder
'un peu de' ile karıştırılmamalı: 'peu' yetersizliği vurgular
o kadar çok, bu kadar çok

tables.caption_tr: Measurement and Container Expressions (same rule with de)
rows: un kilo de pommes (bir kilo elma)
une bouteille de lait (bir şişe süt)
une tasse de thé (bir fincan çay)
un morceau de gâteau (bir dilim pasta)
une tranche de pain (bir dilim ekmek)
une boîte de chocolats (bir kutu çikolata)
un paquet de sucre (bir paket şeker)

tables.caption_tr: Golden Rule: Article Drops, Only 'de' Remains
rows: Su içiyorum. → Çok fazla su içiyorum.
footnotes_tr: Before nouns starting with a vowel (a, e, i, o, u) or silent 'h', 'de' → 'd' (élision): d'eau, d'amis, d'idées.

tables.caption_tr: Countable or Uncountable? — Usage Differences
footnotes_tr: 'quelques' (a few) is an indefinite adjective, not a quantitative adverb; therefore it does not take 'de': quelques amis (not BEAUCOUP DE quelques DE amis!).

tables.caption_tr: Exceptions: Structures Where the Article Does Not Drop

footnotes_tr: These exceptions are not 'quantitative adverb + de' pattern, but 'noun + de' pattern (bien, plupart, majorité are nouns); therefore the normal 'de + les → des' rule applies.

y-en-pronouns.intro_tr: Y and en are two special pronouns used in French to prevent the repetition of certain preposition groups. Y generally replaces the structure "à + place" or "à + thing" (not used for people); en replaces the structure "de + place/thing", partial articles (du, de la, des), and quantity expressions. Both are placed in the sentence immediately before the conjugated verb (in affirmative imperative, after the verb, connected with a hyphen). These pronouns, extremely frequently used in spoken language, also form the basis of many fixed expressions like "il y a", "vas-y", "j'en ai marre".

tables.caption_tr: Uses of Y
rows: Bir yere gitme, bir yerde bulunma
Diğer yer edatları da y ile karşılanır
Kişiler için vurgulu zamir (moi, toi, lui, elle...) kullanılır

tables.caption_tr: Uses of En

Kişi için vurgulu zamir tercih edilir; bazı kalıplarda (parler de qqn) en de kabul edilir

J'y suis allé(e). / J'en ai mangé.
Je vais y aller. / Je vais en manger.
Je dois y penser. / Je peux en prendre.
N'y + fiil + pas / N'en + fiil + pas
N'y va pas ! / N'en mange pas !
footnotes_tr: -er verbs normally drop -s in the tu imperative form (va, mange), but -s returns before y or en for ease of pronunciation: vas-y, manges-en.

imparfait.intro_tr: Imparfait is a past tense in French used to express actions that are ONGOING, REPEATED, or DESCRIPTIVE in the past; it corresponds to the Turkish "-yordu" (was continuing) and "-erdi/-ardı" (habit) meanings. Unlike Passé composé, when the action starts and when it ends is not important — what matters is the action being "ongoing." That is why imparfait is used when describing past weather, person/place descriptions, habits, and the background of an event. Its conjugation is very easy: almost without exception, every verb is derived from the "nous" stem of the present tense and the same 6 endings are added. The only true exception is the stem "ét-" of the verb être.

tables.caption_tr: Imparfait Personal Endings (Common for All Verbs)
footnotes_tr: Rule: from the verb's present tense 'nous' conjugation, '-ons' is removed, and these endings are added to the remaining stem. Ex: nous parl-ons → parl- + ais.
-ais, -ais, -ait, -aient are all pronounced with the same [ɛ] sound in pronunciation; only the spelling is different.

tables.caption_tr: Full Conjugation of Regular Verbs (-er, -ir, -re Groups)
footnotes_tr: In -ir verbs like finir, the stem is in the form 'finiss-' (derived from the present tense nous finiss-ons).

tables.caption_tr: Conjugation of the Verb être (Only Irregular Stem)
footnotes_tr: In French, the only verb with an irregular stem in the imparfait is être (stem: ét-); the endings are still standard.
All other verbs (including avoir) follow the rule: nous av-ons → j'avais, tu avais, il avait...

tables.caption_tr: Uses of the Imparfait
rows: Chaque été, nous allions à la mer. (Her yaz denize giderdik.)
Kişi, yer, hava durumu, duygu tasviri
Il faisait froid et le ciel était gris. (Hava soğuktu, gökyüzü griydi.)
Passé composé'deki ani olayın arka planı
Je dormais quand tu as appelé. (Sen aradığında ben uyuyordum.)
Pendant ce temps, elle travaillait. (Bu esnada o çalışıyordu.)
Je voulais vous poser une question. (Size bir soru sormak istiyordum.)
Gerçek dışı/varsayımsal koşul, sonuç conditionnel présent'te
Si j'avais de l'argent, je voyagerais. (Param olsaydı seyahat ederdim.)

tables.caption_tr: Comparison of Passé Composé and Imparfait
rows: Il a plu. (Yağmur yağdı — tamamlanmış olay)
toujours, souvent, chaque jour, autrefois, d'habitude
soudain, un jour, tout à coup, une fois, tout de suite
footnotes_tr: The two tenses are typically used together in the same sentence: imparfait sets the scene, passé composé narrates the event.

relative-pronouns.intro_tr: Relative pronouns (pronoms relatifs) are linking words that combine two sentences into one sentence, preventing repetition; they correspond to adjectival participle suffixes in Turkish (-en, -dığı, etc.). "Qui" is the subject, "que" is the object (COD), and "dont" replaces verb/noun/adjective structures that require the preposition "de"; "où" indicates place and time. These four pronouns are the most frequently used, basic relative pronouns in French, and their correct selection is critical for sentence clarity. Which pronoun is selected depends on whether the word in the second sentence being combined is a subject, object, or a complement with a preposition. This page summarizes the usage areas of the four basic pronouns and common mistakes in table format; prepositional structures (lequel vb.) and advanced topics like ce qui/ce que are addressed on a separate page.

tables.caption_tr: General Overview of Relative Pronouns
rows: L'homme qui chante est mon voisin. (Şarkı söyleyen adam komşumdur.)
Le film que j'ai vu était nul. (İzlediğim film kötüydü.)
de + isim/fiil/sıfat yapısı (parler de, avoir besoin de, content de...)

Bir yer adı veya zaman ifadesi

'le jour où', 'au moment où', 'l'année où' gibi ifadelerde kullanılır

depuis-pendant-il-y-a.title_tr: Time Expressions: depuis, pendant, il y a, dans
depuis-pendant-il-y-a.intro_tr: In French, to express time, depuis, pendant, il y a and dans are used according to four different logics and cannot be used interchangeably. depuis describes a situation that started in the past and is still ongoing, and is generally used with présent (meaning "-since, -for" in Turkish). pendant specifies a period with a clear beginning and end, completed (or to be completed) (meaning "during, throughout"). il y a indicates precisely when something happened in the past (meaning "... ago") and is always used with passé composé/passé. dans, on the other hand, indicates when something will happen in the future from the present moment (meaning "... later") and is used with futur. Confusing these four is one of the most common mistakes Turkish students make, because in Turkish they can sometimes all be expressed with similar suffixes like "-de/-dır/-önce/-sonra".

tables.caption_tr: General Overview: The Basic Difference of Four Time Expressions
rows: Her zaman kipiyle kullanılabilir (geçmiş, şimdi, gelecek) — eylem TAMAMLANMIŞ ya da tamamlanacak
Sürenin başı ve sonu belli, kapalı bir aralık
Şu andan gelecekteki bir noktaya kadar
footnotes_tr: il y a here means 'ago'; 'il y a' is also a separate impersonal structure that means 'there is/are' (see Impersonal Structures), and should not be confused.

tables.caption_tr: depuis: Two Different Ways of Use
rows: Eylemin NE KADAR ZAMANDIR devam ettiğini belirtir
Je travaille ici depuis trois ans.
'...den beri ...memiş/yapmamış' — passé composé + depuis birlikte kullanılabilir çünkü eylemin YOKLUĞU şimdiye kadar sürüyor
Je n'ai pas dormi depuis deux jours.
depuis'nin konuşma dilindeki alternatifi, cümle başında kullanılır
Ça fait trois ans que j'habite ici.
Eşanlamlı yapı: voilà/il y a ... que

tables.caption_tr: dans and en Comparison (Frequently Confused!)
rows: ... sonra (gelecekte belirli bir ana kadar bekleme süresi)
Eylem henüz başlamamış, bir süre SONRA başlayacak

Eylemin başından sonuna kadar geçen TOPLAM süreyi belirtir
Il a fait ce travail en dix minutes.
footnotes_tr: In short: dans = 'when will it start', en = 'in how much time will it be completed/was it completed'.

tables.caption_tr: pendant, depuis, en Comparison: Same Sentence, Different Meaning
rows: J'ai vécu à Lyon pendant cinq ans.

gerondif.intro_tr: Gérondif is a verbal-adverb structure formed with the pattern "en + verb-ant" in French, which is not conjugated at all according to the subject. It corresponds to the Turkish suffixes "-erek/-arak" (e.g., "koşarak") or "-ken" (e.g., "giderken"). It is used to express a second action that the subject of the main clause performs at the same time; with meanings of simultaneity, method, reason, or condition. The pattern "tout en + gérondif" generally adds a meaning of contrast or emphasis (e.g., "despite/in spite of"). Golden rule: the implicit subject of the gérondif must always be the same person as the subject of the main clause; otherwise, the gérondif cannot be used.

connectors-basic.title_tr: Conjunctions: parce que, donc, pourtant, alors que
connectors-basic.intro_tr: In French, conjunctions (les connecteurs logiques) link two sentences or ideas together, showing the logical relationship between them. "parce que" and similar ones indicate reason, "donc" and similar ones indicate result, "pourtant" and similar ones indicate unexpected contrast, and "alors que" indicates both opposition and simultaneity. The position of each conjunction in the sentence, the register (colloquial/formal), and punctuation rules differ; therefore using them interchangeably as if they "mean the same thing" often leads to errors. On this page, four main conjunctions and their closest synonyms (car, puisque, comme, alors, cependant, tandis que) are presented comparatively.

tables.caption_tr: General Overview of Conjunction Categories
rows: parce que / car → iki cümle arasında; comme → daima cümle başında
donc, alors, par conséquent, c'est pourquoi
iki cümle arasında veya cümle başında
ama, yine de, ancak, buna rağmen
footnotes_tr: These four conjunctions (parce que, donc, pourtant, alors que) are the most frequently used at B1 level; synonyms such as car, puisque, comme, cependant, tandis que are also compared in the table.

tables.caption_tr: Reason Conjunctions: parce que, car, puisque, comme Differences
rows: Yeni/asıl bilgi verir; 'Pourquoi?' sorusuna doğrudan cevap olabilir
Je suis content parce que j'ai réussi.
İki bağımsız cümle arasında, virgül veya noktalı virgülle
Yazı dilinde yaygın; asla cümlenin en başında kullanılmaz
Il n'est pas venu, car il était malade.
Konuşan ile dinleyenin zaten bildiği açık bir sebebi hatırlatır, 'madem' anlamı verir
Puisque tu insistes, je viens avec toi.
Sebep cümlesi ana cümleden önce gelir; özellikle yazılı anlatımda tercih edilir
Comme il pleuvait, nous sommes restés chez nous.
footnotes_tr: 'parce que' can be used alone as a short answer to the question 'Pourquoi?': 'Pourquoi tu pleures? — Parce que je suis triste.'
'car' is not used at the beginning of a sentence; in this position 'comme' is preferred.

tables.caption_tr: Result Conjunctions: donc, alors, par conséquent, c'est pourquoi
rows: Cümle ortasında (özneden sonra) ya da başında
Nötr; hem yazı hem konuşma dilinde kullanılır
Il pleut, donc je prends un parapluie.
Il pleut, alors je reste à la maison.
Les ventes ont baissé ; par conséquent, les prix ont augmenté.
Il a menti ; c'est pourquoi personne ne lui fait confiance.
Il a raté le bus, du coup il est arrivé en retard.

tables.caption_tr: Contrast Conjunctions: pourtant, mais, cependant Differences
rows: En temel ve en sık kullanılan karşıtlık bağlacı

Cümle başında veya ortasında, genelde ikinci (sonuç) cümlede
Beklenmedik/şaşırtıcı bir karşıtlığı vurgular ('yine de, buna rağmen')
Il a beaucoup révisé ; pourtant, il a raté l'examen.
Cümle başında, nokta veya noktalı virgülden sonra
Daha resmî ve edebî; 'mais'ten daha güçlü bir zıtlık bildirir

Çok günlük konuşma dili, 'yine de' anlamı verir
Il pleuvait, on est sortis quand même.
footnotes_tr: 'pourtant' is an independent adverbial conjunction; unlike 'bien que' or 'quoique', it does not take 'que' after it and does not require the subjunctive.

tables.caption_tr: Two Basic Meanings of alors que
rows: İki durum arasındaki tersliği veya farkı gösterir ('oysa, halbuki')

footnotes_tr: After alors que, the normal indicative mood is used, not the subjunctive.
tandis que is almost synonymous with alors que but is more often preferred in written language.

Comme il pleuvait, je suis resté. / Je suis resté, car il pleuvait.
'car' asla cümle başında kullanılmaz; sebep cümle başında yer alacaksa 'comme' tercih edilir.

'pourtant' bağımsız bir zarftır; 'bien que'nin aksine 'que' almaz.

Il travaille alors qu'il est fatigué.
'alors que' + indicatif kullanılır, subjonctif değil (bien que'nin aksine).
Donc parce qu'il pleut, je reste.
Parce qu'il pleut, je reste. / Il pleut, donc je reste.
'donc' (sonuç) ve 'parce que' (sebep) aynı cümlede birlikte, aynı işlev için kullanılmaz.

plus-que-parfait.title_tr: Plus-que-parfait (Past of the Past) — Comprehensive Guide
plus-que-parfait.intro_tr: Plus-que-parfait is a tense that corresponds to the Turkish "-mIştI" suffix and is called "past of the past": it expresses another event that occurred BEFORE the event narrated in the past. Structurally, it is constructed with the IMPARFAIT form of the auxiliary verb avoir or être + the participe passé (past participle) — that is, it is the "past tense shifted back one step" of passé composé. The most frequent places of use are: clarifying the order of two past events, in indirect speech (concordance des temps) moving passé composé to the past, and with the pattern "si + plus-que-parfait, ... conditionnel passé" to express unrealized past conditions / regrets. In verbs taking être and in reflexive verbs, the rules for participle agreement are identical to those in passé composé.

tables.caption_tr: 1. Formation — Plus-que-parfait with avoir (example: parler)
footnotes_tr: The imparfait conjugation of the auxiliary verb avoir (avais, avais, avait, avions, aviez, avaient) + the participe passé of the verb is used.
The vast majority of French verbs are conjugated with avoir.

tables.caption_tr: 2. Formation — Plus-que-parfait with être and Gender/Number Agreement (example: aller)
footnotes_tr: In verbs conjugated with être, the participe passé, just as in passé composé, agrees in gender and number with the SUBJECT.

tables.caption_tr: 3. Verbs Taking the être Auxiliary (Movement/Change of State Verbs)
footnotes_tr: Memory aid abbreviation: DR & MRS VANDERTRAMP (each letter is the initial of a verb).
The derived forms of these verbs (repartir, redescendre, etc.) generally also take être.
Reflexive (pronominal) verbs are also always conjugated with être: s'était levé(e), s'étaient couché(e)s.

tables.caption_tr: 4. Participe Passé (Past Participle) Agreement Rules
rows: COD (belirtili nesne) fiilden ÖNCE gelirse, participe COD ile uyumlu olur.
La pomme qu'elle avait mangée était verte.
Participe her zaman ÖZNE ile uyumlu.
COD dönüşlü zamirse özne ile uyumlu; zamir COD değilse (dolaylı nesneyse) uyumsuz.
Elle s'était lavée. / Elle s'était lavé les mains.
footnotes_tr: These rules are identical to the participle agreement rules in passé composé.

tables.caption_tr: 5. Areas of Use
rows: Anlatılan geçmiş olaydan ÖNCE gerçekleşen ikinci bir olayı belirtir.
Quand elle est arrivée, nous avions déjà mangé.
Ana cümle geçmiş zamandaysa, aktarılan passé composé plus-que-parfait olur.
Il a dit qu'il avait vu ce film. (← 'J'ai vu ce film')
'Si + plus-que-parfait, ... conditionnel passé' kalıbıyla gerçekleşmemiş geçmiş varsayım.
Si tu m'avais appelé, je serais venu.
Genelde 'si seulement' ile birlikte geçmişe dönük pişmanlık anlatır.
Si seulement j'avais écouté mes parents !
Bir durumun sebebini geçmişte daha önceki bir olayla açıklar.
Il était fatigué parce qu'il n'avait pas dormi.

tables.caption_tr: 6. Common Mistakes
rows: avoir ile être karıştırılmamalı; hareket fiilleri être alır.
arriver être alan bir fiildir, avoir değil.
Il avait mangeait avant de partir.
Il avait mangé avant de partir.
Yardımcı fiilden sonra participe passé gelir, imparfait değil.
Les fleurs qu'il avait acheté étaient belles.
Les fleurs qu'il avait achetées étaient belles.
COD (les fleurs) fiilden önce geldiği için ortaç dişil-çoğul uyumlu olmalı.
Plus-que-parfait ile imparfait'i eş zamanlı olay için kullanmak.
İki eş zamanlı geçmiş olay için imparfait kullanılır, plus-que-parfait değil.
Plus-que-parfait yalnızca DAHA ÖNCE biten bir olay için kullanılır.

subjonctif-present.title_tr: Introduction to Subjonctif Présent (il faut que...)
subjonctif-present.intro_tr: Subjonctif présent in French does not express a fact that has occurred; rather, it is a mood that expresses a subjective perspective such as necessity, desire, emotion, doubt, or permission. It is almost always used after the conjunction "que", depending on a triggering expression in the main clause. The most common and easiest introductory pattern is the structure "il faut que..." (must..., need to...): "Il faut que tu partes" = "You need to leave." On this page you will find the formation rule of subjonctif présent, complete conjugations of the most frequently used regular and irregular verbs, triggering expressions, and situations confused with the indicative. Regarding tense, subjonctif présent is used for both present and future actions; there is no separate "subjonctif futur".

tables.caption_tr: Formation Rule: Personal Endings
rows: Çoğu fiilde -e sesi telaffuz edilmez (parle gibi)
Telaffuz edilmez, je ile aynı okunur
Telaffuz edilmez, présent indicatif ile aynı okunur
footnotes_tr: General rule: stem = remove -ent from the ils/elles présent form (ils parlent → parl-). Verbs such as être, avoir, aller, faire, pouvoir, savoir, vouloir, falloir are exceptions to this rule.

tables.caption_tr: Complete Conjugation of Regular Verbs (parler, finir, vendre)
footnotes_tr: In -ir verbs, -iss- is additionally added to the stem (finir → finiss-), just as in the plural persons of présent indicatif.

tables.caption_tr: Basic Irregular Verbs: être, avoir, aller, faire
footnotes_tr: être and avoir are completely irregular; their stems must be memorized. In aller and faire, only the nous/vous forms use a different stem.

tables.caption_tr: Other Frequently Used Irregular Verbs: pouvoir, savoir, vouloir, falloir
footnotes_tr: falloir is used only in the impersonal form (il faut / qu'il faille); it has no conjugation in other persons.

tables.caption_tr: Verbs with Different Stems in nous / vous
footnotes_tr: In these verbs, the singular persons and ils/elles use the same stem as in présent indicatif (ils boivent → boive), while nous/vous use the imparfait stem (nous buvons → buvions).

tables.caption_tr: il faut que and Other Triggering Expressions
rows: Il est important que vous sachiez cela.
Il vaut mieux que nous partions tôt.
Je souhaite que tu ailles bien.
footnotes_tr: After these expressions, if the subject of the main clause and the subject of the subordinate clause are different, the subjonctif is used; if the subjects are the same, the infinitive is generally preferred instead of 'que': 'Il faut partir' (general) vs. 'Il faut que je parte' (specific subject).

tables.caption_tr: Subjonctif or Indicative? Frequently Confused Cases
rows: Kesinlik bildirir: Je pense qu'il vient.
ne pas penser que / ne pas croire que
Şüphe bildirir: Je ne pense pas qu'il vienne.
il est certain que / il est sûr que
Kesinlik: Il est certain qu'il pleut.
il est possible que / il se peut que
Olasılık: Il est possible qu'il pleuve.
İstisna: Umut olsa da indicatif alır: J'espère qu'il viendra.
Belirsizlik: Il semble qu'il soit fatigué.
Kişisel kanaat kesinlik gibi algılanır: Il me semble qu'il est fatigué.
footnotes_tr: General principle: expressions indicating certainty/reality take the indicative, expressions indicating doubt/emotion/desire/necessity take the subjonctif.

interrogative-pronouns.intro_tr: In French, question pronouns change based on whether what is being asked is a "person" or an "object/thing" and their function in the sentence (subject, object, after preposition). "Qui" is used for people, while "que/quoi" is used for things; "qu'est-ce qui" and "qu'est-ce que" are the long forms (and less formal, also comfortably used in spoken language) of these roots. "Lequel/laquelle/lesquels/lesquelles" on the other hand is a pronoun meaning "which one" that expresses choosing from a previously mentioned group, and must agree with the noun it modifies in gender and number. Although this topic may seem complex at the B1 level, the tables below make it easier to select the correct form by determining whether the question is "who/what" and its function in the sentence.

tables.caption_tr: Question pronouns for people (qui-based) — 'Who?'
rows: Qui vient ce soir ? / Qui est-ce qui vient ce soir ?
Qui vois-tu ? / Qui est-ce que tu vois ?
Edat + qui est-ce que + özne + fiil
À qui parles-tu ? / À qui est-ce que tu parles ?
footnotes_tr: "Qui" always carries the meaning of a person; it is never used for inanimate objects.
Long forms (with est-ce que) allow the sentence to be constructed in normal order without requiring inversion, which is why they are preferred in everyday speech.

tables.caption_tr: Question pronouns for things (que/quoi-based) — 'What?'
rows: Que fais-tu ? / Qu'est-ce que tu fais ?
Edattan sonra (ne ile, neyle, ne hakkında...)
Edat + quoi est-ce que + özne + fiil
De quoi parles-tu ? / De quoi est-ce que tu parles ?
footnotes_tr: "Que" can never be used as a subject; in the subject position, "qu'est-ce qui" is always required.
"Quoi" is always used after a preposition or at the end of a sentence/on its own; it cannot be a subject on its own at the beginning of a sentence.

tables.caption_tr: Lequel / Laquelle / Lesquels / Lesquelles — 'Which one?' complete conjugation table
footnotes_tr: "Lequel" must agree in gender and number with the noun it modifies (the person/object group implied in the question).
It is used when selecting from a group/list: 'Lequel de ces films veux-tu voir ?' (Which of these films do you want to watch?)

tables.caption_tr: Lequel's contracted (fused) forms with the prepositions à and de
footnotes_tr: Feminine forms do not contract (à + laquelle, de + laquelle remain as they are); only masculine and plural forms contract.
Example: 'Auquel de tes collègues fais-tu confiance ?' (Which of your colleagues do you trust?)

tables.caption_tr: Frequently confused points: qui / que / quoi / qu'est-ce que in which case?
rows: Qui vient ? / Qui est-ce qui vient ?
❌ Qu'est-ce que se passe ? / ❌ Que se passe ?
Şey öznesi için 'que' tek başına kullanılamaz, mutlaka 'qu'est-ce qui' gerekir.
İsim tekrarını önlemek için 'quel' değil 'lequel' zamiri kullanılır; 'quel' her zaman bir ismi doğrudan niteler (quel livre?).

conditionnel-present.intro_tr: The conditionnel présent is a mood in French that has two basic functions: (1) politeness — to express requests, suggestions and wishes politely (Je voudrais, Pourriez-vous...) and (2) hypothesis — constructed with the structure "si + imparfait", to describe situations that are not real or difficult to achieve in the present (Si j'avais..., je ferais...). Its conjugation is easy: the future simple stem + the personal endings of imparfait (-ais, -ais, -ait, -ions, -iez, -aient) are combined. Some frequently used verbs (être, avoir, aller, faire, pouvoir, vouloir, devoir, savoir, venir...) have irregular stems and must be memorized. Additionally, in journalism, the conditionnel présent is also used to give "unverified news" (like le ministre démissionnerait demain).

tables.caption_tr: How is Conditionnel Présent Formed? (Stem + Ending)
footnotes_tr: Rule: Conditionnel présent = Future simple stem + Personal endings of imparfait.
In -er and -ir verbs, the stem is generally the infinitive itself (parler-, finir-); in -re verbs the final 'e' drops (vendr-).

tables.caption_tr: Full Conjugation of Regular Verbs (parler, finir, vendre)
Frequently Used Irregular Stems
footnotes_tr: Only the stem is irregular; the endings (-ais, -ais, -ait, -ions, -iez, -aient) are always the same.

tables.caption_tr: Uses of Conditionnel Présent
rows: İsteği doğrudan değil, nazikçe ifade eder
Si j'étais riche, j'achèterais une maison.
J'aimerais visiter le Japon un jour.
Le président serait en visite à Paris.
On pourrait faire un effort, non ?

tables.caption_tr: Ready-Made Patterns for Politeness
Si + Imparfait + Conditionnel Présent (Hypothetical Unreal - Type 2)
rows: Si j'avais de l'argent, je voyagerais.
Param olsaydı seyahat ederdim (şu an param yok).
Je serais content si tu venais.
Sinemaya gitsek nasıl olur? (teklif kalıbı, conditionnel gerekmez)
footnotes_tr: VERY IMPORTANT RULE: The conditionnel NEVER comes immediately after 'si'! Only imparfait, présent or plus-que-parfait can follow.
This structure is used for unreal/unlikely situations in the present or future; for the past, 'si + plus-que-parfait + conditionnel passé' is used (see Conditionnel Passé).

tables.caption_tr: Confused Moods: Futur Simple vs Conditionnel Présent vs Conditionnel Passé
rows: Demain, j'irai au marché. (Yarın pazara gideceğim.)
Kibarlık, öneri, şimdiki zamanda gerçek dışı varsayım

Geçmişte gerçekleşmemiş, pişmanlık ifade eden varsayım

footnotes_tr: Common mistake: saying 'Si j'aurais...' is WRONG; the correct form is 'Si j'avais...' (the conditionnel does not come after si).

examples.note_tr: Politeness: polite invitation/question, preferred instead of 'voulez-vous' in formal settings.

indirect-speech.title_tr: Indirect Speech and Tense Concordance (Discours indirect / Concordance des temps)
indirect-speech.intro_tr: Indirect speech (discours indirect) is to convey someone else's utterance within one's own sentence using conjunctions like "que, si, ce que..." — similar to Turkish structures. In French, the most critical rule of indirect speech is tense concordance (concordance des temps): if the reporting verb (dire, demander, etc.) is in the PAST tense, then the verb of the reported clause also shifts backwards according to a specific pattern (présent→imparfait, futur→conditionnel, etc.); if the reporting verb is in the PRESENT tense, then there is no tense change. Additionally, subject pronouns, possessive adjectives, and time/place adverbials (aujourd'hui, hier, demain, ici...) change according to context. When questions are converted to indirect speech, inversion and the question mark disappear, but the question word (où, quand, pourquoi...) is retained; in yes/no questions "si" is used, and in "qu'est-ce que/qui" questions "ce que/ce qui" is used. This page presents both tense shifts and pronoun/adverbial/conjunction changes together in a single table.

tables.caption_tr: 1. Tense Concordance — When the Main Verb (dire, demander...) is in the PAST Tense
rows: « Je suis malade » → qu'il était malade
« Je vais partir » → qu'il allait partir
Subjonctif présent (il faut que tu viennes)
footnotes_tr: Golden rule: If the reporting verb is in the PRESENT TENSE or FUTURE TENSE (dit, dira) → there is NO tense change, only subject/possessive may change.

tables.caption_tr: 2. Changes in Time and Place Adverbials
footnotes_tr: These changes are mandatory only when the reporting verb is in the PAST tense and the reported event is in the past; if the speech is in the present tense, the adverbials remain unchanged.

tables.caption_tr: 3. Changes in Subject Pronoun and Possessive Adjective
rows: il / elle (ya da je, muhataba göre)
ils / elles (ya da nous, bağlama göre)

tables.caption_tr: 4. Conjunction Selection — According to Sentence Type
rows: « Je viens. » → Il dit qu'il vient.
« Est-ce que tu viens ? » → Il demande si je viens.
Soru kelimeli soru (où, quand, comment, pourquoi, qui, combien)
« Où vas-tu ? » → Il demande où je vais.
« Qu'est-ce qui se passe ? » → Il demande ce qui se passe.
« Que fais-tu ? » → Il demande ce que je fais.
« Viens ! » → Il me dit de venir.
« Ne pars pas ! » → Il me dit de ne pas partir.
footnotes_tr: In indirect questions, inversion is removed, the sentence returns to straight subject-verb order, and a question mark is not used: « Où habites-tu ? » → Il demande où j'habite (not est-ce que ~ 'j'habite où').

tables.caption_tr: 5. Frequently Used Reporting Verbs (Verbes Introducteurs)
rows: demander si / ce que / soru kelimesi

examples.target: Il dit qu'il est fatigué.
examples.translation_tr: He/She says that he/she is tired.
examples.note_tr: Direct: « Je suis fatigué. » Since the main verb (dit) is in the present tense, tense DOES NOT CHANGE; only subject 'je' → 'il' changes.

examples.target: Il a dit qu'il était fatigué.
examples.translation_tr: He/She said that he/she was tired.
examples.note_tr: Direct: « Je suis fatigué. » Since the main verb is in the past (a dit), présent (suis) → imparfait (était) changed.

examples.target: Elle a dit qu'elle avait fini son travail.
examples.translation_tr: He/She said that he/she had finished his/her work.
examples.note_tr: Direct: « J'ai fini mon travail. » Passé composé → plus-que-parfait; 'mon' → 'son'.

examples.target: Il a promis qu'il viendrait le lendemain.
examples.translation_tr: He/She promised to come the next day.
examples.note_tr: Direct: « Je viendrai demain. » Futur simple → conditionnel présent; 'demain' → 'le lendemain'.

examples.target: Il m'a demandé où j'habitais.
examples.translation_tr: He/She asked me where I lived.
examples.note_tr: Direct: « Où habites-tu ? » The question word (où) is retained, inversion and the question mark disappear, présent → imparfait.

examples.target: Il m'a demandé si je venais.
examples.translation_tr: He/She asked me if I was coming.
examples.note_tr: Direct: « Est-ce que tu viens ? » In yes/no questions, 'si' conjunction is used, not 'que'.

examples.target: Il m'a dit de fermer la porte.
examples.translation_tr: He/She told me to close the door.
examples.note_tr: Direct: « Ferme la porte ! » The imperative mood becomes 'de + infinitive' in indirect speech.

examples.target: Il m'a demandé ce que je faisais.
examples.translation_tr: He/She asked me what I was doing.
examples.note_tr: Direct: « Qu'est-ce que tu fais ? » 'Qu'est-ce que' becomes 'ce que' in indirect speech.

tout-usage.title_tr: Uses of tout (tout, toute, tous, toutes)
tout-usage.intro_tr: "tout" is a very versatile word that can be used as an adjective, pronoun, adverb, and even a noun in French; therefore its form (tout, toute, tous, toutes) changes depending on its role in the sentence. As an adjective (determiner), it agrees with the noun in gender and number: tout le monde, toute la classe, tous les jours, toutes les filles. As a pronoun, it means "everything" or "everyone/all" and the plural masculine form "tous" is pronounced in this case (/tus/), whereas in the adjective form the final -s is silent. As an adverb, it means "completely, very" and generally does not change, but before a feminine adjective beginning with a consonant it takes the form toute/toutes. On this page, you will learn to distinguish all four uses with tables.

tables.caption_tr: tout as an Adjective (Determiner) — Complete Conjugation Table
footnotes_tr: When used as an adjective, 'tout' typically appears with a definite article (le, la, les) or a possessive/demonstrative adjective: tout ce livre, toute cette histoire, tous mes amis.

tables.caption_tr: tout as a Pronoun — 'Everything / Everyone / All'
footnotes_tr: IMPORTANT DIFFERENCE: When the pronoun 'tous' is used, the final -s is pronounced (/tus/); when the adjective 'tous' is used (tous les...), the -s is silent. This is the only way to distinguish them by ear.

tables.caption_tr: tout as an Adverb — 'Completely, Very, Entirely'
rows: Dişil sıfat, sesli harf veya sessiz 'h' ile başlıyor
Dişil sıfat, 'h aspiré' (aspire h) ile başlıyor
footnotes_tr: Rule logic: In French, to avoid consecutive vowel sounds (like tout + étonnée), the adverb remains unchanged; but in consonant clashes, the 'toute/toutes' form is preferred to sound more fluid.
'h muet' (silent h) behaves like a vowel, 'h aspiré' (aspirated h) behaves like a consonant — it is marked with an * in the dictionary.

tables.caption_tr: tout in Idiomatic Expressions
rows: tout à coup / tout d'un coup
Tout à coup, il a crié.
Je ne suis pas du tout fatigué.
Ils sont venus tous les deux.
Il est venu tout de même.

tables.caption_tr: Frequently Confused Points and Comparisons
rows: Ils sont tous là (/tus/) — tous les jours (sessiz s)
'tout/tous' grubu bir bütün olarak ele alır; 'chaque' her bireyi tek tek vurgular.
tous les élèves (bütün öğrenciler) — chaque élève (her bir öğrenci)
tout le + tekil isim vs tous les + çoğul isim
'tout le' = bütün/tüm (tek bir varlık); 'tous les' = her (tekrarlanan)
tout le mois (bütün ay boyunca) — tous les mois (her ay, aylık)
'tout' tek başına isim olarak 'bütün, tamamı' anlamında kullanılabilir.

examples.translation_tr: She cleaned the whole house. (toute = feminine singular adjective)

examples.reading: tous /tus/
examples.translation_tr: All of them came to the party.
examples.note_tr: Here 'tous' is used as a pronoun, so the -s is pronounced (/tus/); this is the difference from its adjective use.

examples.translation_tr: Completely surprised by the news.
examples.note_tr: Since 'étonnée' begins with a vowel, the adverb 'tout' remains unchanged.
