examples.target: Paul aime le vin ; Marie, la bière.
examples.reading: Pol em lö ven; Mari, la biyer.
examples.translation_tr: Paul loves wine; Marie (loves) beer.
examples.note_tr: In the second sentence, the repeated verb 'aime' is omitted, and a comma is used in its place — a classic example of gapping.

examples.target: Il se leva et partit sans un mot.
examples.reading: İl sö löva e parti san-en mo.
examples.translation_tr: He/She stood up and left without saying a word.
examples.note_tr: The common subject 'il' is not repeated before the second verb.

examples.target: Elle est plus intelligente que lui (ne l'est).
examples.reading: El e plüz enteliijant kö lüi (nö le).
examples.translation_tr: He/She is more intelligent than him/her.
examples.note_tr: In the comparison, the repeated adjective 'intelligent(e)' is omitted in the second part; 'ne l'est' is also usually dropped in everyday speech.

examples.target: — Tu viens ce soir ? — Si possible.
examples.reading: Tü vyen sö swar? Si posibl.
examples.translation_tr: — Are you coming tonight? — If possible.
examples.note_tr: The full form would be 'si c'est possible'; in the conditional clause, the subject + verb are omitted.

examples.target: Moi aussi, j'adore le chocolat.
examples.reading: Mwa osi, jador lö şokola.
examples.translation_tr: I also really love chocolate.
examples.note_tr: 'Moi aussi' can also be used alone: the full form 'j'aime aussi' is omitted.

examples.target: — Je ne suis pas d'accord. — Moi non plus.
examples.reading: Jö nö süi pa dakor. Mwa non plü.
examples.translation_tr: — I don't agree. — Neither do I.
examples.note_tr: Agreement with a negative sentence formula; it is an abbreviation of the full sentence 'je ne suis pas d'accord non plus'.

examples.target: — Qui a cassé le vase ? — Le chat.
examples.reading: Ki a kase lö vaz? Lö şa.
examples.translation_tr: — Who broke the vase? — The cat (did).
examples.note_tr: Question-answer ellipsis: the verb and complement are not repeated, only the new information (subject) is given.

examples.target: Il faut partir maintenant, sinon on sera en retard.
examples.reading: İl fo partir mentnan, sinon on söra an rötar.
examples.translation_tr: We need to leave now, otherwise we'll be late.
examples.note_tr: 'Sinon' by itself replaces an entire conditional clause meaning 'si ce n'est pas le cas / si on ne le fait pas'.

inversion-styles.title_tr: Inverted Structures and Stylistic Inversion (peut-être est-il...)
inversion-styles.intro_tr: In French, while the normal sentence order is subject-verb (il est), in formal writing and literary style, when certain adverbs or structures come at the beginning of the sentence, the subject and verb swap places: instead of "il est" it becomes "est-il". This is called stylistic (stylistique) inversion and, unlike inversion in interrogative sentences, it does not carry a question meaning; it merely adds formality and fluency to the written language. Adverbs like "peut-être", "sans doute", "aussi" (meaning "for this reason"), "à peine", "du moins" trigger this inverted structure when they come at the beginning of a sentence. Additionally, inversion also appears in dialogues with reporting verbs (dire, répondre, s'écrier) and in some fixed conditional/optative clauses. This structure frequently appears at C1 level, especially when reading and writing newspapers, novels, and formal texts.

tables.caption_tr: Sentence-Initial Adverbs That Trigger Inversion
rows: Il était à peine arrivé qu'il repartit.
À peine était-il arrivé qu'il repartit.
Il en reste tout au plus dix.
Tout au plus en reste-t-il dix.
footnotes_tr: When 'aussi' is used in the middle of a sentence, inversion is not required; inversion is only done when the conjunction is used at the beginning of a sentence meaning 'for this reason'.
These adverbs are generally expressed without inversion in spoken language, using simpler conjunctions like 'donc/alors'; the inverted structure is specific to written language.

tables.caption_tr: Types of Inversion: Simple and Complex Inversion
rows: Özne zaten zamirse doğrudan yer değiştirir.
Fiil sesli harfle bitiyorsa 3. tekil şahısta araya -t- girer
'a', 'va', 'parle' gibi ünlü ile biten fiillerde telaffuz kolaylığı için -t- eklenir.
İsim özne yerinde kalır + fiilden sonra ona karşılık gelen zamir eklenir
Özne bir isim/isim öbeğiyse tekrar zamirle özetlenir; isim düşürülmez.
Yardımcı fiil (avoir/être) + zamir, ortaç sonda kalır
Sadece yardımcı fiil özne ile yer değiştirir, geçmiş ortaç yerinde durur.

tables.caption_tr: Inversion in Dialogue with Reporting Verbs (dit-il structure)
rows: "Gidiyorum" dedi Paul. (isim öznede tekrar zamir eklenmez)
"Bekle" diye sakin bir sesle cevap verdi.
footnotes_tr: This structure is standard in speech reporting in novels and stories; it is not used in everyday spoken language, only appears in writing.

tables.caption_tr: Condition Without 'Si': Fixed Conditional Clauses with Inverted Structure
rows: Eût-il su la vérité, il serait resté.
S'il avait su la vérité, il serait resté.
Gerçeği bilseydi, kalırdı. (subjonctif plus-que-parfait ile devrik)
Fût-ce le dernier jour, elle viendrait.
Même si c'était le dernier jour, elle viendrait.
Son gün bile olsa, o gelirdi.
Même s'il devait tout perdre, il continuerait.
Her şeyini kaybetse bile devam ederdi.
Même s'il était riche, il resterait simple.
footnotes_tr: These structures are fixed expressions at a very high literary/formal level; they carry the meaning of 'même si' and are generally constructed with subjunctive imperfect/pluperfect forms.
It is almost never used in everyday language; recognition in C1-C2 text reading is sufficient.

Cümle başında 'peut-être' varsa ya inversiyon yapılmalı ya da zarf cümle içine taşınmalı; ikisi birden olmaz.
Ünlü ile biten fiil + zamir arasına '-t-' eklenmesi unutulmamalı.

Diyalog aktarımında fiil-özne sırası her zaman devriktir, normal sıra kullanılmaz.
İsim özne kullanıldığında zamir tekrar eklenmelidir (karmaşık inversiyon); isim tek başına fiilden sonra bırakılmaz.

concession-opposition.title_tr: Concession and Contrast: bien que, quoique, avoir beau
concession-opposition.intro_tr: Concession structures are used to express that a situation does not prevent an expected result: like "Despite being tired, he continues working." In French, this meaning can be expressed with conjunctions like bien que / quoique (always with subjunctive), with the avoir beau + infinitive pattern, or with prepositional phrases like malgré / en dépit de. Understanding which structure requires subjunctive, indicative, or infinitive is critical for natural and error-free expression at C1 level. Additionally, the difference between quoique (one word, conjunction) and quoi que (two words, "whatever ... may be") is one of the most frequently confused points. This page presents all structures, mood rules, agreement tables, and typical errors together.

tables.caption_tr: Main Concession Conjunctions Requiring Subjunctive
rows: bien que ile eşanlamlı, tek kelime yazılır
Dilbilgisel olarak eleştirilir; yazıda malgré + isim tercih edilmeli
İstisna: bu yapı çoğunlukla indicatif alır

tables.caption_tr: avoir beau + Infinitive: Conjugation in All Tenses (example verb: essayer)
rows: Il a beau essayer, il échoue.
Il avait beau essayer, il échouait.
Il a eu beau essayer, il a échoué.
Il aura beau essayer, il échouera.
Il aurait beau essayer, il échouerait.
footnotes_tr: After avoir beau, the infinitive comes directly; the conjunction 'que' is not used and subjunctive is not required.

tables.caption_tr: quoique (conjunction, one word) vs quoi que (indefinite + que, two words)
rows: Belgisiz zamir + que (= her ne ... olursa)
Quoi que tu dises, je ne te crois pas.
footnotes_tr: Both require subjunctive; the difference is in meaning and spelling, not in pronunciation.

tables.caption_tr: Concession/Contrast Expressions Formed with Preposition + Noun
rows: En dépit des difficultés, elle a réussi.

tables.caption_tr: quel(le)(s) que + être (Subjunctive) — Complete Agreement Table

Quelles que soient les conditions, nous partirons.
footnotes_tr: quel/quelle/quels/quelles agrees with the subject in gender and number; soit/soient are always the subjunctive present forms of the verb être and come immediately before the subject.

tables.caption_tr: Conjunction, Preposition, or Adverb? Mood and Structure Comparison
rows: Bien qu'il soit riche, il est avare.
Même s'il est riche, il est avare.

Il est avare, alors qu'il est riche.

examples.target: Malgré la pluie, nous sommes sortis nous promener.
examples.translation_tr: Despite the rain, we went for a walk.

examples.target: Quel que soit le résultat, nous serons fiers de toi.
examples.translation_tr: Whatever the outcome may be, we will be proud of you.
examples.note_tr: quel agrees with the subject (le résultat → masculine singular); soit is always the subjunctive être.

examples.target: Quoi que tu fasses, je te soutiendrai toujours.
examples.translation_tr: Whatever you do, I will always support you.
examples.note_tr: quoi que (two words) = 'whatever ... may be'; requires subjunctive (faire → fasses).

examples.target: Même si tu as raison, tu dois rester poli.
examples.translation_tr: Even if you are right, you must remain polite.
examples.note_tr: même si always takes indicative (avoir → as); subjunctive is an error.

examples.target: Si intelligent qu'il soit, il fait parfois des erreurs.
examples.translation_tr: However intelligent he may be, he sometimes makes mistakes.
examples.note_tr: si + adjective + que + subjunctive; used in literary/written contexts.

punctuation-style.title_tr: Orthography and Punctuation Subtleties (dash, guillemets, spacing rules)
punctuation-style.intro_tr: French written language has its own distinctive punctuation and typographic rules; these are distinctly different from Turkish and English. The most striking difference is that a space (thin/espace insécable) is left BEFORE punctuation marks like ; : ! ?. Moreover, « » (guillemets) are used instead of quotation marks for quotations, long dash (—) is preferred in dialogues, comma is used in decimal numbers, and space is used in thousand grouping. This page summarizes in table form all these orthographic and punctuation subtleties frequently encountered when producing formal/literary text at C1 level.

tables.caption_tr: Punctuation Marks and Spacing Rules (Specific to French)
footnotes_tr: In French, the space left before punctuation marks ; : ! ? is called 'espace insécable' (thin/indivisible space); this is a fundamental difference from Turkish and English.
In Canadian French (Québec), in some publishing rules this before-space application is more flexible.

literary-registers.intro_tr: Literary style is based on special tenses and inverted sentence structures used in French novels, historical texts, official speeches, and classical literature; no longer living in everyday conversation. In this register, passé simple is preferred instead of passé composé, passé antérieur sometimes instead of plus-que-parfait, and imparfait/plus-que-parfait du subjonctif instead of subjonctif présent/passé. Furthermore, in sentences beginning with adverbs like peut-être, sans doute, aussi, à peine, subject-verb inversion occurs (inversion stylistique). These structures are almost never used in modern spoken French, but they are mandatory for understanding/writing literature, history, and official texts. The tables below summarize all the conjugations and usage rules of this "literary French".

tables.caption_tr: Literary Narrative Tenses — Fields of Use and Everyday Language Equivalents
rows: Anlatıda tamamlanmış tekil olay (roman, tarih, masal)
Passé simple'dan hemen önce biten eylem (quand, dès que, à peine que ile)
Ana cümle geçmiş zamandayken subjonctif gerektiren yan cümle
Geçmişte tamamlanmış varsayımsal/duygusal eylem; edebî 2. tip koşul (si'siz)
Peut-être, sans doute, aussi, à peine gibi zarflardan sonra vurgu
footnotes_tr: Passé composé and subjonctif présent/passé replace literary tenses in everyday and semi-official writing.

tables.caption_tr: Passé Simple — Complete Conjugation Table
footnotes_tr: -er verbs take -ai/-as/-a/-âmes/-âtes/-èrent; most -ir/-re verbs take -is/-is/-it/-îmes/-îtes/-irent.

tables.caption_tr: Imparfait du Subjonctif — Complete Conjugation Table (derived from passé simple stem)
footnotes_tr: The 3rd singular person (il/elle) form always ends with circumflex accent (^): parlât, finît, fût, eût — this form is seen only in very formal/literary texts today.

tables.caption_tr: Adverbs and Conjunctions Triggering Stylistic Inversion
rows: Il pleuvait, aussi resta-t-elle chez elle.
Yağmur yağıyordu, bu yüzden evde kaldı.
À peine était-il arrivé qu'il repartit.
Daha yeni varmıştı ki tekrar gitti.
Ainsi parlait-il souvent de son passé.
footnotes_tr: After these adverbs at the beginning of a sentence, subject-verb is inverted; in 3rd singular/plural person, if necessary, -t- is added in impersonal verbs (viendra-t-il).

tables.caption_tr: Comparison of Everyday Language and Literary Language
rows: Il avait déjà mangé quand elle est arrivée.
Il eut déjà mangé quand elle arriva.
Il est parti, donc elle est restée seule.
S'il avait su, il n'aurait rien dit.
Eût-il su, il n'aurait rien dit.
footnotes_tr: The structures in the right column are valid only in written/literary texts; they are not used when speaking.

examples.target: Il naquit à Paris en 1802 et mourut en 1885.

examples.target: Quand il eut fini son discours, l'assemblée applaudit.
examples.translation_tr: When he finished his speech, the assembly applauded. (passé antérieur + passé simple agreement)

examples.target: Elle souhaitait qu'il fût plus prudent.
examples.translation_tr: He wished he were more careful. (imparfait du subjonctif)

examples.target: À peine eut-elle refermé la porte que le téléphone sonna.

examples.target: Peut-être reviendra-t-il un jour.

examples.target: Sans que nul ne s'en aperçût, il quitta la salle.

examples.target: Ainsi vécut-il jusqu'à la fin de ses jours.
examples.translation_tr: Thus he lived until the end of his days. (ainsi + inversion)

examples.target: Eût-il su la vérité, il n'aurait rien dit.
examples.translation_tr: Even if he had known the truth, he would have said nothing. (plus-que-parfait du subjonctif, if-less conditional)

passe-anterieur.title_tr: Passé Antérieur and Literary Tense Agreement
passe-anterieur.intro_tr: Passé antérieur is a compound past tense unique to literary and formal writing; it describes a second action completed JUST BEFORE an event expressed in the main clause with passé simple (giving the meaning 'no sooner...than', 'barely...when'). It is used almost exclusively after temporal conjunctions like quand, lorsque, dès que, aussitôt que, après que, à peine... que, when the main clause also contains passé simple. In everyday spoken language, plus-que-parfait (or passé composé) takes its place. Passé antérieur, together with passé simple + subjonctif imparfait + subjonctif plus-que-parfait, is part of French's "literary tense system" (concordance des temps littéraire) and appears in genres like classic novels, historical texts, and formal narratives. At the C2 level, the goal is not to PRODUCE this tense, but to RECOGNIZE and correctly interpret it in literary texts.

tables.caption_tr: Passé Antérieur Conjugation — Complete Example (parler: with avoir / aller: with être)
rows: il fut allé / elle fut allée
ils furent allés / elles furent allées

tables.caption_tr: Formation Formula: Auxiliary Verb in Passé Simple Form + Participe Passé
rows: avoir: j'eus, tu eus, il eut, nous eûmes, vous eûtes, ils eurent
être: je fus, tu fus, il fut, nous fûmes, vous fûtes, ils furent
il se fut couché / elle se fut couchée

tables.caption_tr: Temporal Conjunctions That Trigger Passé Antérieur
rows: Quand il eut mangé, il sortit.
Après qu'il eut parlé, tout le monde se tut.
Dès qu'ils furent arrivés, on commença.
Aussitôt qu'elle eut lu la lettre, elle pleura.
À peine eut-il fini qu'on l'appela.
Une fois qu'il eut compris, il agit.
footnotes_tr: If 'À peine' is at the beginning of the sentence, inversion (the subject and verb change places) is obligatory: À peine eut-il ouvert... With other conjunctions, normal word order is used.
The verb in the main clause is almost always passé simple; passé antérieur is not used on its own without a main clause.

tables.caption_tr: Literary Tense Agreement (Concordance des Temps Littéraire): Written Language vs. Spoken Language
rows: il eut fini → il avait fini
qu'il eût fini → qu'il ait fini
eût-il su, il fût venu → s'il avait su, il serait venu
footnotes_tr: In the literary system, all tenses are interconnected: passé simple establishes the main framework, passé antérieur [describes] the action immediately before it, and subjonctif imparfait/plus-que-parfait conveys the mood in dependent clauses.
This table is for C2 reading/comprehension; PRODUCING these structures in speech is not expected, only recognizing them in 19th–20th century literature is necessary.

tables.caption_tr: Examples of Passé Antérieur with Frequently Used Irregular Participe Passé
rows: il fut né / elle fut née
il fut mort / elle fut morte
il fut venu / elle fut venue
il fut devenu / elle fut devenue

tables.caption_tr: Common Mistakes
rows: Quand il a fini, il partit.
Ana cümle passé simple iken yan cümlede passé composé edebî uyuma aykırıdır.
Quand il eut fini, il partit.
Il eut fini son travail. (tek başına)

Dönüşlü fiillerde yardımcı fiil être'dir, avoir değil.
Modern konuşmada 'Dès qu'il eut fini, on partit.'

examples.target: Quand il eut fini son travail, il partit.

examples.note_tr: When 'À peine' is at the beginning of the sentence, subject-verb inversion (eut-il) is used; this is a typical feature of literary prose.

examples.note_tr: With reflexive verbs (se coucher), passé antérieur is constructed with être and participle agreement: se fut couché.

francophone-varieties.title_tr: Francophone Differences: Québec, Belgium and Swiss French
francophone-varieties.intro_tr: French is spoken not only in France; in Québec (Canada), Belgium and Switzerland it is also an official language, and each region has its own unique vocabulary, number system, pronunciation habits and certain grammar trends. These differences generally appear in everyday spoken language, slang and regional expressions; official/written standard French is largely the same. A C2 level student should be able to recognize these variations encountered both in written texts and authentic audio/video sources, and should eliminate the risk of misunderstanding or thinking it is 'incorrect French'. The tables below systematically summarize the most frequently encountered differences in numbers, words, grammar, forms of address and interjections. The aim is not to produce these variants but to recognize and understand them — in exams and official correspondence, standard (French) French is still the basis."

tables.caption_tr: Regional Differences in Numbers (70-99)
footnotes_tr: In Switzerland, 'huitante' is common only in the Vaud and Fribourg cantons; in Geneva and other regions 'quatre-vingts' is used.
In exams and official writing, the standard French form (soixante-dix, quatre-vingts, quatre-vingt-dix) is the basis.

archaic-fixed-forms.title_tr: Frozen Old Structures (fût-il, d'aucuns, n'eût été)
archaic-fixed-forms.intro_tr: These structures are fossilized inverted expressions specific to French's literary, legal, and journalistic language, almost never used in everyday speech. They are generally constructed using subject-verb inversion of the subjunctive imperfect and carry concessive and conditional meanings such as 'even though...', 'if... had not...', and 'in order to...'. These patterns are no longer productive; that is, new sentences cannot be freely derived from them, and they are only recognized and used as memorized fixed expressions. At the C2 level, recognizing these structures is necessary for understanding classical literature, legal texts, and high-level press language; in everyday usage, their place is taken by modern equivalents like "même si", "sans", "certains".

subjonctif-plus-que-parfait.title_tr: Subjonctif Plus-que-parfait and Second Conditionnel Passé (2e Forme)
subjonctif-plus-que-parfait.intro_tr: Subjonctif plus-que-parfait is the most literary and rarest tense-mood combination in French; in everyday speech it is almost never heard, appearing only in classical literature, historical narratives, and very formal/legal texts. It has two main functions: (1) in sentences requiring tense agreement (concordance des temps), subjonctif imparfait is used as the past-of-the-past equivalent; (2) in the usage called "2e forme" (second form), in both the si condition clause and the result clause, it replaces conditionnel passé, conveying the same meaning in a much more noble/literary style. It is important to recognize this structure because it appears frequently in 19th-century novels (Balzac, Flaubert, Proust); however, in modern French it is NOT used productively—knowledge for READING comprehension is sufficient. The form is created by adding participe passé to the subjonctif imparfait conjugation (eusse/fusse) of avoir/être verbs.

tables.caption_tr: Subjonctif Imparfait Conjugation of Auxiliary Verbs (eusse / fusse) — This is the foundation of plus-que-parfait
footnotes_tr: Subjonctif plus-que-parfait = auxiliary verb in this table + participe passé (fait, allé, parlé...).
The circumflex accent (accent circonflexe) above 3rd person singular forms like 'eût', 'fût' is a distinguishing feature; they should not be confused with 'eut', 'fut' (passé simple).

tables.caption_tr: Complete Conjugation Example: parler (with avoir) and aller (with être)
footnotes_tr: In conjugations with être, participe passé agrees in gender/number with the subject (just as in normal passé composé).
Reflexive verbs are also conjugated with être as the auxiliary verb: qu'il se fût levé.

nested-subclauses.title_tr: Nested Subordinate Clauses and Long-Distance Dependencies
nested-subclauses.intro_tr: One characteristic feature of formal and literary expression in French is the nesting of subordinate clauses within each other and the establishment of a bridge between an element in the main clause (subject, triggering verb, conjunction) and an element in a distant subordinate clause (verb mood, pronoun, reference). This "nesting" (enchâssement) is typically formed by using relative clauses (qui, que, dont, où, lequel), complement clauses (que), and adverbial clauses (bien que, alors que, quand) in sequence or nested within one another. The difficulty lies in tracking, as sentences grow longer, what element pronouns refer to (antecedent) and how the element that triggers mood selections like subjonctif maintains its effect despite intervening clauses. At C2 level, the goal is to both correctly parse and understand these structures and to produce them in readable form in written/formal style. The tables below summarize types of nesting, layered patterns, rules for distant mood/tense agreement, and strategies for maintaining clarity.

idiomatic-structures.intro_tr: In French, idiomatic patterns (expressions idiomatiques) and proverbs (proverbes), which cannot be translated word-for-word, are frozen expressions with a fixed word order and often a special grammatical structure. These structures range from idioms constructed with basic verbs like avoir, faire, être to proverb patterns like "qui...", "tel... tel..." with omitted subjects and subordinate clauses. At the C2 level, recognizing both the meaning of these patterns and the archaic (archaïque) syntax hidden within them — subjonctif, inverted structure, article omission — is essential for advanced reading, writing, and speaking skills. These expressions cannot be altered: when word order, article usage, or verb mood is disrupted, meaning is lost or the sentence sounds artificial; therefore, they must be memorized as whole units.

stylistic-inversion.title_tr: Stylistic Inversion and Heavy Element Displacement
stylistic-inversion.intro_tr: Stylistic inversion (l'inversion stylistique) is the removal of subject-verb order from normal sequence in French's written and literary style; it is almost never used in everyday speech but is very frequently seen in newspapers, literature, and formal texts. There are two main sources of this inversion: (1) certain adverbs and conjunctions that come at the beginning of a sentence (peut-être, ainsi, sans doute, à peine...) trigger subject-verb inversion; (2) "heavy element displacement" (when the subject is very long/complex, moved to the end of the sentence) is used to facilitate information flow — this is called in linguistics "extraposition" or "heavy subject postposition". Inversion can take two forms: the subject comes directly after the verb (simple inversion) or the subject remains in place and a clitic pronoun is added to the verb (complex inversion). At the C2 level, this structure will constantly appear in academic writing and literary text reading/writing, so mastery is required.

footnotes_tr: These adverbs trigger inversion only when used at the beginning of a sentence (or at the beginning of a subordinate clause); if used in the middle/end of the sentence, normal word order is preserved (e.g., 'Il a peut-être raison' — no inversion).

rows: İkincisi yazı diline ve resmî üsluba özgüdür; anlam aynı, sadece biçem farkı.
Une lettre inattendue est arrivée hier soir.
Est arrivée hier soir une lettre inattendue.
Devrik cümle, yeni bilgiyi (lettre) vurgulamak için sona atar; anlatı/gazetecilik dilinde yaygın.
Mon grand-père habitait autrefois dans cette maison.
La maison où habitait autrefois mon grand-père...
İlgi cümleciğinde ağır özne (mon grand-père) fiilden sonraya kayar, cümle daha dengeli okunur.
Il faut le prouver quand même.
Devrik yapı daha resmî/yazınsal bir ton katar, konuşma dilinde nadirdir.
Elle était à peine sortie quand le téléphone sonna.
À peine était-elle sortie que le téléphone sonna.
'à peine...que' kalıbı devrik olmadan da kullanılabilir ama yazı dilinde devrik biçim tercih edilir.

tables.caption_tr: Common Mistakes and Correct Usage
rows: Peut-être a-t-il raison. / Il a peut-être raison.
Peut-être cümle başındaysa devrik zorunludur; devrik istenmiyorsa peut-être cümle içine/sonuna alınmalı.
3. tekil şahısta özne zamiri ve fiil ünlüyle karşılaşırsa araya '-t-' konur.
Il est arrivé hier soir. / Est arrivé un homme étrange hier soir.
Ağır kaydırma yalnızca isim/isim öbeği öznelerle yapılır, zamir öznelerle yapılmaz.
Ainsi parlait-il. / Ainsi il parlait. (konuşma dilinde)
Edebî/yazınsal metinlerde 'ainsi' sonrası devrik beklenir; konuşma dilinde devriksiz de kabul edilir ama biçemsel değildir.

Özne isim olduğunda karmaşık inversiyonda özne TEKRARLANMAZ olarak zamirle değiştirilmez, sadece klitik zamir eklenir; iki özne birden (Marie + elle) yan yana çift özne hatası yapılmamalı — doğrusu: özne isim + fiil + tireli klitik zamir.

examples.target: Peut-être pleuvra-t-il demain.
examples.translation_tr: Perhaps tomorrow it will rain. (subject-verb inversion after peut-être: pleuvra-t-il)

examples.target: Ainsi s'acheva leur long voyage à travers l'Europe.
examples.translation_tr: Thus ended long journeys lasting across Europe. (simple inversion: verb + noun subject)

examples.target: À peine était-elle sortie que le téléphone sonna.
examples.translation_tr: Scarcely had he gone out when the phone rang. (mandatory inversion in the à peine ... que pattern)

examples.target: Sans doute a-t-il raison de s'inquiéter.
examples.translation_tr: No doubt he/she was right to be worried. (sans doute + complex inversion: a-t-il)

examples.target: Est arrivée hier soir une lettre venue d'un pays lointain.
examples.translation_tr: Yesterday evening a letter coming from a distant country arrived. (heavy subject 'une lettre venue d'un pays lointain' was displaced to after the verb)

examples.target: Reste à savoir si cette solution, proposée par plusieurs experts internationaux, sera acceptée.
examples.translation_tr: It remains to be known whether this solution recommended by many international experts will be accepted. (Heavy subject phrase was displaced to after the verb)

examples.target: Le livre que lisait patiemment mon vieux professeur de littérature était introuvable.
examples.translation_tr: The book that my literature teacher was patiently reading could not be found. (heavy subject inversion in the relative clause: que lisait mon vieux professeur)

examples.target: Encore faut-il que tout le monde soit d'accord.
examples.translation_tr: Still everyone must be in agreement. (encore + complex inversion, continues with subjunctive)
